AL-001.topic: Systemic reaction to an insect sting
AL-001.stem_html:
A 42-year-old man comes to the office 1 week after an emergency department visit. While gardening he was stung on the hand by a yellow jacket. Within 10 minutes he developed generalized hives, throat tightness, wheezing and lightheadedness. Paramedics gave intramuscular epinephrine, and he recovered fully after observation. He had local swelling after a bee sting as a child. He has hypertension treated with amlodipine.

Examination today is normal.
AL-001.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.A: Prescribe an oral antihistamine to take after any future sting
choices.B: Prescribe daily oral prednisone during the summer months
choices.C: Prescribe an epinephrine autoinjector and refer for venom skin testing and immunotherapy
choices.D: Advise avoidance of outdoor activity; no prescription is needed
choices.E: Prescribe an epinephrine autoinjector only; no further evaluation is needed

AL-001.explain_html:
Correct answer: C Systemic reaction to an insect sting

He had anaphylaxis from a hymenoptera sting: skin involvement plus respiratory and cardiovascular symptoms within minutes. Without treatment, the chance of a similar or worse reaction to a future sting is about 30%–60% in adults.

Two steps protect him:

  1. Epinephrine autoinjector (two devices), with training to use it immediately for any systemic reaction and then call emergency services.
  2. Referral to an allergist for venom-specific IgE or skin testing and venom immunotherapy (VIT). VIT reduces the risk of a future systemic reaction to under 5% and is usually continued for 3–5 years.
Reaction to a sting Venom testing & immunotherapy?
Large local reaction (swelling >10 cm, contiguous) Not routinely
Cutaneous-only systemic reaction (adults) Consider (shared decision)
Anaphylaxis (respiratory or cardiovascular) Yes

Why not the others

  • (A) Prescribe an oral antihistamine to take after any future sting — Antihistamines treat itching and hives but do not reverse airway edema or hypotension; they are never a substitute for epinephrine.
  • (B) Prescribe daily oral prednisone during the summer months — Prophylactic glucocorticoids do not prevent sting anaphylaxis and cause harm.
  • (D) Advise avoidance of outdoor activity; no prescription is needed — Avoidance is advised but not reliable, and he needs epinephrine available.
  • (E) Prescribe an epinephrine autoinjector only; no further evaluation is needed — An autoinjector alone leaves him at high risk; immunotherapy is the only treatment that changes the natural history.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Beta-blockers can make anaphylaxis harder to treat (epinephrine resistance — give glucagon); ACE inhibitors may worsen reactions during venom immunotherapy. Review his medications before VIT.

🎯 Educational objective

After a systemic (anaphylactic) reaction to an insect sting, prescribe an epinephrine autoinjector and refer for venom testing and venom immunotherapy.

CV-001.stem_html:
A 49-year-old man comes to the office to review his blood pressure log. Three months ago his office blood pressure was 158/96 mm Hg. Since then he has cut back on salt, walks 30 minutes most days and has lost 2 kg (4.4 lb). His validated home cuff now shows an average of 156/98 mm Hg over the last 2 weeks. He has no symptoms. He does not have diabetes and does not smoke. His father had a myocardial infarction at age 61.

Blood pressure in the office today is 154/97 mm Hg in both arms; pulse is 74/min. BMI is 29 kg/m². Cardiac examination is normal and there is no edema.

Sodium140 mEq/L
Potassium4.3 mEq/L
Creatinine0.9 mg/dL
Urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio12 mg/g
LDL cholesterol128 mg/dL
CV-001.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.C: Continue lifestyle changes and recheck blood pressure in 6 months
choices.E: Start a single-pill combination of an angiotensin receptor blocker and amlodipine

CV-001.explain_html:
Correct answer: E Essential hypertension

This man has confirmed stage 2 hypertension (home average ≥140/90 mm Hg) that persists despite 3 months of lifestyle change. His goal is <130/80 mm Hg.

When blood pressure is ≥140/90 mm Hg (or more than about 20/10 mm Hg above goal), one drug is rarely enough. Current US guidance recommends starting two first-line drugs from different classes at the same time, preferably as a single-pill combination. Two half-doses lower pressure more than one full dose, cause fewer dose-related side effects, and one pill improves adherence.

The first-line classes are thiazide-type diuretics, ACE inhibitors or ARBs, and dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers. An ARB + amlodipine pill is a standard choice; ACE inhibitor or ARB + thiazide is equally acceptable.

Office BP Plan
130–139 / 80–89 Lifestyle; add one drug if CVD, diabetes, CKD or high 10-year risk
≥140 / 90 Lifestyle plus two first-line drugs, ideally one pill
≥180 / 120 with organ damage Hypertensive emergency → hospital, IV therapy

Why not the others

  • (A) Start hydralazine — Hydralazine is a late add-on (resistant hypertension, pregnancy, HFrEF with nitrate). It causes reflex tachycardia and fluid retention when used alone.
  • (B) Start lisinopril plus losartan — ACE inhibitor + ARB together (dual RAAS blockade) raises the risk of hyperkalemia and acute kidney injury without cardiovascular benefit. Never combine them.
  • (C) Continue lifestyle changes and recheck blood pressure in 6 months — He has already tried lifestyle change for 3 months and remains far above goal. Waiting 6 more months leaves stage 2 hypertension untreated.
  • (D) Start atenolol — Beta-blockers are not first-line for uncomplicated hypertension. They prevent fewer strokes than the first-line classes; use them when there is another indication (angina, prior MI, HFrEF, rate control).
🧠 Mnemonic

"A-C-D" — the three first-line classes: ACE inhibitor/ARB, Calcium channel blocker (dihydropyridine), Diuretic (thiazide-type). Stage 2 → pick two of the three.

🎓 ABIM pearl

Confirm office readings with home or ambulatory monitoring before diagnosing hypertension. Office-only elevation is white-coat hypertension; normal office but high home readings is masked hypertension, which carries the same risk as sustained hypertension.

🎯 Educational objective

For confirmed stage 2 hypertension (≥140/90 mm Hg), start two first-line antihypertensives from different classes, preferably as a single-pill combination, and target <130/80 mm Hg.

CV-002.stem_html:
A 61-year-old woman comes to the office for a routine visit. She ran out of her amlodipine and chlorthalidone 8 days ago and did not refill them. She feels well. She has no headache, chest pain, dyspnea, visual change or weakness.

Blood pressure is 194/112 mm Hg, rechecked after 10 minutes of quiet rest at 190/110 mm Hg; pulse is 78/min. She is alert and oriented. Fundoscopic examination shows mild arteriolar narrowing without hemorrhages, exudates or papilledema. Heart and lung examination is normal, and neurologic examination is nonfocal.

Creatinine1.0 mg/dL (baseline 1.0 mg/dL)
Urinalysisno blood or protein
ECGsinus rhythm; left ventricular hypertrophy by voltage (unchanged from 1 year ago)
CV-002.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.A: Obtain a noncontrast CT scan of the head
choices.B: Give oral clonidine every hour until blood pressure is below 140/90 mm Hg
choices.D: Give intravenous labetalol in the emergency department
choices.E: Restart her home medications and recheck blood pressure within 1 week

CV-002.explain_html:
Correct answer: E Severe asymptomatic hypertension

This is severe asymptomatic hypertension (formerly "hypertensive urgency"): blood pressure ≥180/110–120 mm Hg without acute target-organ damage. Her fundi, kidneys, ECG and neurologic examination show no acute injury. The cause is obvious — she stopped her medicines.

The danger in this situation is lowering the pressure too fast. Chronic hypertension shifts cerebral and coronary autoregulation to the right. A sudden drop can cause stroke, myocardial ischemia or acute kidney injury. Short-term risk from the elevated pressure itself is low.

Correct care: restart (or intensify) oral therapy, aim to lower blood pressure gradually over days to weeks, and arrange close follow-up. ED referral and IV drugs are for hypertensive emergency, when organ damage is present.

Severe asymptomatic HTN Hypertensive emergency
Organ damage None acute Encephalopathy, stroke, ACS, pulmonary edema, AKI, dissection, retinal hemorrhage/papilledema
Setting Office / outpatient ICU
Drugs Oral IV (nicardipine, clevidipine, labetalol, esmolol)
Pace Over days–weeks ≤25% in the first hour (faster for dissection)

Why not the others

  • (A) Obtain a noncontrast CT scan of the head — She has no neurologic symptoms or signs. Imaging is not needed without features of encephalopathy or stroke.
  • (B) Give oral clonidine every hour until blood pressure is below 140/90 mm Hg — Rapid oral loading to a normal pressure within hours is the same error as IV therapy, and clonidine stacking causes rebound hypertension later.
  • (C) Give immediate-release nifedipine sublingually now — Immediate-release nifedipine causes abrupt, unpredictable drops in pressure and has caused stroke and MI. It should not be used for this purpose.
  • (D) Give intravenous labetalol in the emergency department — IV antihypertensives are for hypertensive emergency. Using them without organ damage risks hypotension and hypoperfusion and adds no benefit.
🎓 ABIM pearl

The number alone does not make an emergency — organ damage does. Look at the eyes, brain, heart, lungs and kidneys before you reach for an IV drug.

🎯 Educational objective

Severe hypertension without acute target-organ damage is treated with oral medication and gradual lowering over days to weeks with close outpatient follow-up, not with rapid or IV blood pressure reduction.

CV-003.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
CV-003.explain_html:
Correct answer: E Complete heart block

The strip shows third-degree (complete) AV block: P waves march at their own regular rate and wide QRS complexes march at a slower, independent rate — there is no relationship between them. Bedside clues fit: cannon a waves (atria contract against a closed tricuspid valve) and a variable S₁.

She has symptomatic complete heart block with syncope (Stokes-Adams attacks) and a wide escape rhythm, which means the block is below the AV node and the escape is unreliable. Once reversible causes are excluded, the treatment is a permanent pacemaker (Class 1). Her labs exclude hyperkalemia, hypothyroidism and acute MI, and lisinopril does not slow AV conduction.

Reversible causes to check before pacing
AV-nodal drugs: beta-blockers, nondihydropyridine CCBs, digoxin, amiodarone
Hyperkalemia
Acute inferior MI (often transient)
Lyme carditis (young patient, tick exposure)
Hypothyroidism, increased vagal tone, obstructive sleep apnea

Why not the others

  • (A) Tilt-table testing — Tilt-table testing evaluates reflex (vasovagal) syncope. Her syncope is arrhythmic and already explained.
  • (B) 30-day ambulatory event monitor — The diagnosis is already made on the strip. More monitoring only delays treatment of a rhythm that can cause sudden death.
  • (C) Oral theophylline — Theophylline is occasionally used for post-transplant bradycardia or as a temporary bridge. It is not a treatment for infranodal complete heart block.
  • (D) Stop lisinopril and observe — ACE inhibitors do not block the AV node. Stopping lisinopril would not correct complete heart block.
🧠 Mnemonic

Third-degree block: "P's and Q's don't agree" — atria and ventricles keep their own time.

🎓 ABIM pearl

A narrow escape (40–60/min) suggests block in the AV node (more stable). A wide escape (20–40/min) suggests infranodal block (His–Purkinje) — unstable, and atropine usually does not help.

🎯 Educational objective

Symptomatic complete heart block without a reversible cause is an indication for permanent pacemaker implantation.

CV-004.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate therapy to reduce her risk of stroke?

choices.C: No antithrombotic therapy because her heart rate is controlled
choices.D: Warfarin with a target INR of 2.0–3.0

CV-004.explain_html:
Correct answer: B Atrial fibrillation — stroke prevention

The ECG shows atrial fibrillation: irregularly irregular R–R intervals and no discrete P waves.

Stroke risk in AF depends on the patient, not on the rhythm or rate. Her CHA₂DS₂-VASc score is 3 (age 65–74 = 1, hypertension = 1, female sex = 1). Anticoagulation is recommended when annual stroke risk is ≥2%, which corresponds to a score of ≥2 in men or ≥3 in women (female sex is a risk modifier — it counts only when other factors are present).

For eligible patients, a direct oral anticoagulant (DOAC) is preferred over warfarin: equal or better stroke prevention, about half the intracranial hemorrhage, no INR monitoring. DOACs are not used with a mechanical valve or moderate–severe rheumatic mitral stenosis — warfarin is the drug there.

CHA₂DS₂-VASc Points
CHF or LV dysfunction 1
Hypertension 1
Age ≥75 2
Diabetes 1
Stroke / TIA / thromboembolism 2
Vascular disease (MI, PAD, aortic plaque) 1
Age 65–74 1
Sex category (female) 1

Why not the others

  • (A) Aspirin plus clopidogrel — Dual antiplatelet therapy is inferior to anticoagulation for AF stroke prevention and carries similar bleeding risk.
  • (C) No antithrombotic therapy because her heart rate is controlled — Rate control treats symptoms, not stroke risk. Stagnant flow in the left atrial appendage persists however well the rate is controlled.
  • (D) Warfarin with a target INR of 2.0–3.0 — Warfarin works, but DOACs are preferred because they cause less intracranial hemorrhage and need no INR monitoring. Warfarin is the right choice only for a mechanical valve or moderate–severe mitral stenosis.
  • (E) Aspirin — Aspirin gives little stroke protection in AF and bleeds almost as much as a DOAC. It is not recommended for stroke prevention in AF.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Calculate HAS-BLED to find and fix modifiable bleeding risks (uncontrolled BP, NSAIDs, alcohol, labile INR) — not to withhold anticoagulation. A high bleeding score is rarely a reason to skip a DOAC.

🎯 Educational objective

In atrial fibrillation, anticoagulate when CHA₂DS₂-VASc is ≥2 in men or ≥3 in women, and prefer a DOAC over warfarin unless the patient has a mechanical valve or moderate–severe mitral stenosis.

CV-005.stem_html:
An 82-year-old man is evaluated for 4 months of breathlessness when he climbs one flight of stairs. Last week he felt lightheaded and had to sit down while carrying groceries. He has hypertension and hyperlipidemia. He lives independently, drives and walks his dog daily.

Blood pressure is 134/78 mm Hg and pulse is 70/min. There is a grade 3/6 late-peaking crescendo–decrescendo systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border that radiates to both carotids. The aortic component of S₂ is soft. Carotid upstrokes are delayed and weak.

Echocardiogram — aortic valve area0.7 cm²
Echocardiogram — mean gradient48 mm Hg
Echocardiogram — peak aortic jet velocity4.6 m/s
Echocardiogram — LV ejection fraction60%
CV-005.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.B: Start a beta-blocker for exertional symptoms
choices.C: Balloon aortic valvuloplasty as definitive therapy

CV-005.explain_html:
Correct answer: E Aortic stenosis

He has severe aortic stenosis (AVA ≤1.0 cm², mean gradient ≥40 mm Hg, peak velocity ≥4.0 m/s) and he is symptomatic (exertional dyspnea and presyncope). Once symptoms appear, average survival without valve replacement is only a few years, and sudden death becomes a real risk. Aortic valve replacement is indicated (Class 1).

No medicine changes the natural history of AS. The question is only which replacement. At age >80, transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) is generally preferred over surgery when anatomy is suitable; for patients <65 with long life expectancy, surgical AVR is usually favored; between those ages, it is a shared decision by the heart team.

Classic symptoms of severe AS Rough survival without AVR
Angina ~5 years
Syncope ~3 years
Heart failure ~2 years

Why not the others

  • (A) Repeat echocardiography in 12 months — Watchful waiting with serial echo is for asymptomatic severe AS with normal LV function. Symptoms change the indication to valve replacement now.
  • (B) Start a beta-blocker for exertional symptoms — Beta-blockers do not relieve the obstruction and can worsen exertional symptoms by limiting the heart rate response.
  • (C) Balloon aortic valvuloplasty as definitive therapy — Balloon valvuloplasty gives only temporary relief (restenosis within months). It is a bridge, not definitive therapy.
  • (D) Start lisinopril to reduce afterload — Vasodilators can drop blood pressure sharply because cardiac output is fixed by the narrowed valve; they do not treat the obstruction.
🧠 Mnemonic

Symptoms of severe AS — "SAD": Syncope, Angina, Dyspnea. Any one of them with severe AS → replace the valve.

🎓 ABIM pearl

A soft or absent A₂ and late-peaking murmur mean severe AS. Murmur loudness is misleading — it falls when the LV fails.

🎯 Educational objective

Symptomatic severe aortic stenosis requires aortic valve replacement; in patients older than 80 years with suitable anatomy, transcatheter implantation is preferred.

CV-006.stem_html:
A 62-year-old man comes for follow-up 6 months after a non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction treated with a drug-eluting stent. He takes aspirin, ticagrelor, metoprolol succinate, lisinopril and atorvastatin 80 mg daily. He reports taking every dose and has no muscle pain. He walks 40 minutes daily and follows a Mediterranean diet.

Blood pressure is 124/76 mm Hg. Examination is normal.

Total cholesterol162 mg/dL
LDL cholesterol88 mg/dL (before the MI 156 mg/dL)
HDL cholesterol42 mg/dL
Triglycerides160 mg/dL
ALT28 U/L
Hemoglobin A1c5.6%
CV-006.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to reduce his cardiovascular risk?
CV-006.explain_html:
Correct answer: C Lipid management after myocardial infarction

He has clinical ASCVD with a recent ACS — very high risk. He is already on a maximally tolerated high-intensity statin, yet his LDL is still ≥70 mg/dL (current expert pathways aim even lower, at <55 mg/dL, for very-high-risk patients).

The next step is a nonstatin drug with outcome data: ezetimibe first (cheap, oral, well tolerated; IMPROVE-IT showed fewer cardiovascular events after ACS). If LDL remains above threshold, add a PCSK9 inhibitor (or inclisiran/bempedoic acid in selected patients).

Lower LDL, longer, is better — every 39 mg/dL (1 mmol/L) reduction in LDL lowers major vascular events by about 20%.

Statin intensity Drug and daily dose LDL reduction
High Atorvastatin 40–80 mg, rosuvastatin 20–40 mg ≥50%
Moderate Atorvastatin 10–20, rosuvastatin 5–10, simvastatin 20–40 30%–49%

Why not the others

  • (A) Add niacin — Niacin raises HDL but did not reduce events on top of a statin (AIM-HIGH, HPS2-THRIVE) and causes flushing, hyperglycemia and myopathy.
  • (B) Switch to rosuvastatin 5 mg daily — Rosuvastatin 5 mg is moderate intensity — a step down from atorvastatin 80 mg.
  • (D) Continue current therapy unchanged — His LDL is above the threshold for adding therapy in very-high-risk ASCVD. Accepting it leaves avoidable risk.
  • (E) Add fenofibrate — Fibrates lower triglycerides; his triglycerides are only mildly elevated and fibrates added to a statin have not reduced cardiovascular events.
🎓 ABIM pearl

After ACS, check a lipid panel 4–12 weeks after starting or changing therapy to confirm response and adherence, then every 3–12 months.

🎯 Educational objective

In very-high-risk ASCVD with LDL ≥70 mg/dL despite a maximally tolerated statin, add ezetimibe and then a PCSK9 inhibitor if needed.

CV-007.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
CV-007.explain_html:
Correct answer: B Acute pericarditis

He meets the diagnosis of acute pericarditis (≥2 of 4): pleuritic, positional chest pain; a pericardial friction rub; diffuse concave ST elevation with PR depression; and a new pericardial effusion. Most cases in young adults are viral or idiopathic.

First-line therapy is a high-dose NSAID (or aspirin) plus colchicine. Colchicine roughly halves the recurrence rate and speeds symptom relief. Typical course: ibuprofen 600 mg three times daily for 1–2 weeks with a taper; colchicine 0.5 mg twice daily (once daily if <70 kg) for 3 months. Restrict strenuous exercise until symptoms and CRP resolve (at least 3 months for athletes).

Admit if any high-risk feature: fever >38 °C, subacute onset, large effusion or tamponade, failure of NSAIDs after 1 week, immunosuppression, trauma, oral anticoagulation, or myopericarditis (elevated troponin).

Why not the others

  • (A) Pericardiocentesis — The effusion is small and there is no tamponade. Pericardiocentesis is for tamponade or suspected bacterial/malignant effusion.
  • (C) Prednisone 1 mg/kg daily — Glucocorticoids as first-line therapy increase recurrences. Reserve them for NSAID contraindications, failure, or specific causes (autoimmune disease, pregnancy constraints).
  • (D) Urgent coronary angiography — Normal troponin, normal wall motion, diffuse (not territorial) ST elevation and PR depression point away from STEMI.
  • (E) Ibuprofen alone — An NSAID alone works but leaves about twice the recurrence risk compared with adding colchicine.
🎓 ABIM pearl

ECG tells pericarditis from STEMI: concave ST elevation in many territories, PR depression, no reciprocal ST depression (except aVR and V1), and no Q waves.

🎯 Educational objective

Treat acute idiopathic or viral pericarditis with a high-dose NSAID plus colchicine for 3 months; avoid first-line glucocorticoids because they increase recurrence.

CV-008.topic: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
CV-008.stem_html:
A 64-year-old man with ischemic cardiomyopathy comes for follow-up. He gets short of breath after walking about two blocks but has no dyspnea at rest, orthopnea or edema. Over the past 6 months his medicines were titrated to sacubitril–valsartan 97/103 mg twice daily, metoprolol succinate 200 mg daily, spironolactone 25 mg daily and furosemide 20 mg daily. He does not have diabetes.

Blood pressure is 112/70 mm Hg and pulse is 60/min, regular. Jugular venous pressure is normal and the lungs are clear. There is no edema. Echocardiography last month showed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 30%.

Sodium138 mEq/L
Potassium4.6 mEq/L
Creatinine1.3 mg/dL (eGFR 58 mL/min/1.73 m²)
Hemoglobin A1c5.7%
CV-008.lead: Which of the following drugs should be added to his regimen?
CV-008.explain_html:
Correct answer: E Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction

Guideline-directed therapy for HFrEF rests on four pillars, each of which lowers mortality: an ARNI (or ACE inhibitor/ARB), an evidence-based beta-blocker, a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist and an SGLT2 inhibitor. He is on three of the four.

Dapagliflozin or empagliflozin reduce cardiovascular death and heart-failure hospitalization by about 25% in HFrEF with or without diabetes (DAPA-HF, EMPEROR-Reduced). Benefit appears within weeks. They can be started down to an eGFR of about 20–25 mL/min/1.73 m², cause little hypotension, and slow kidney function decline.

Pillar Examples Watch for
ARNI (or ACEi/ARB) Sacubitril–valsartan Hypotension, K⁺, angioedema (36-h ACEi washout)
Beta-blocker Carvedilol, metoprolol succinate, bisoprolol Bradycardia, start low when euvolemic
MRA Spironolactone, eplerenone K⁺ >5.0, eGFR <30
SGLT2 inhibitor Dapagliflozin, empagliflozin Genital mycotic infection, euglycemic DKA, volume

Why not the others

  • (A) Hydralazine plus isosorbide dinitrate — Hydralazine–nitrate is added for self-identified Black patients with persistent NYHA III–IV symptoms on optimal therapy, or for patients who cannot take an ARNI/ACE inhibitor/ARB. He fits neither.
  • (B) Ivabradine — Ivabradine is for patients in sinus rhythm whose heart rate stays ≥70/min on a maximally tolerated beta-blocker. His heart rate is 60/min.
  • (C) Digoxin — Digoxin reduces hospitalizations for symptoms but not mortality. It is added only when symptoms persist on full GDMT or for AF rate control.
  • (D) Diltiazem — Nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers are negative inotropes and worsen HFrEF. Avoid them.
🧠 Mnemonic

The four pillars: "Always Be My Shield" — ARNI, Beta-blocker, MRA, SGLT2 inhibitor.

🎓 ABIM pearl

He also meets criteria for a primary-prevention ICD: ischemic cardiomyopathy, EF ≤35%, NYHA II, ≥40 days after MI, on ≥3 months of GDMT, with >1-year expected survival.

🎯 Educational objective

Every patient with HFrEF should receive all four mortality-reducing drug classes — ARNI/ACE inhibitor/ARB, beta-blocker, MRA and an SGLT2 inhibitor — regardless of diabetes status.

choices.A: Photograph the lesion and re-examine in 3 months

DE-001.explain_html:
Correct answer: C Suspected melanoma

The lesion has almost every ABCDE feature of melanoma plus the "ugly duckling" sign — it looks different from the patient's other nevi.

The pathologist needs the whole lesion and its full depth to measure Breslow thickness — the most important prognostic factor — which then determines the definitive wide-excision margin and whether sentinel lymph node biopsy is needed.

In situ 0.5–1 cm

1.01–2.0 mm 1–2 cm

A lesion suspicious for melanoma should be removed by full-thickness excisional biopsy with narrow margins so that Breslow depth can guide definitive treatment.

DE-002.topic: Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS)
DE-002.stem_html:
A 58-year-old woman comes to the emergency department with 4 days of fever and a spreading itchy rash that began on her face and trunk. Allopurinol was started 5 weeks ago for recurrent gout. She has chronic kidney disease. She takes no other new medications.

Temperature is 38.9 °C (102.0 °F), blood pressure is 118/70 mm Hg and pulse is 104/min. There is facial edema and a confluent erythematous morbilliform eruption covering about 60% of the body surface. There are no blisters, skin sloughing or mucosal erosions. Tender cervical and axillary lymphadenopathy is present.

Leukocyte count14,800/µL
Eosinophils1,900/µL
Atypical lymphocytespresent
ALT342 U/L
AST266 U/L
Creatinine2.1 mg/dL (baseline 1.5 mg/dL)
DE-002.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.A: Stop allopurinol and start systemic glucocorticoids
choices.B: Stop allopurinol and switch to febuxostat
choices.C: Stop allopurinol and observe without other treatment
choices.D: Continue allopurinol and add an oral antihistamine
choices.E: Continue allopurinol at a lower dose

DE-002.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS)

Fever, a widespread rash with facial edema, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia, atypical lymphocytes and organ involvement (liver, kidney) starting 2–8 weeks after a new drug is DRESS (drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms). Mortality is up to about 10%, mostly from liver failure.

Management:

  1. Stop the culprit drug immediately — the single most important step.
  2. With significant organ involvement (as here — hepatitis and acute kidney injury), give systemic glucocorticoids (for example prednisone 0.5–1 mg/kg/day) with a slow taper over 6–12 weeks; tapering too fast causes relapse.
  3. Monitor for late complications: autoimmune thyroiditis, type 1 diabetes and reactivation of HHV-6.
Common culprits of DRESS
Allopurinol, aromatic anticonvulsants (carbamazepine, phenytoin, lamotrigine, phenobarbital)
Sulfonamides (including sulfasalazine, dapsone), minocycline, vancomycin

Why not the others

  • (B) Stop allopurinol and switch to febuxostat — Avoid any urate-lowering therapy until DRESS resolves; restarting a related drug during active disease is unsafe. Febuxostat can be considered later with specialist input.
  • (C) Stop allopurinol and observe without other treatment — Stopping the drug is necessary but not enough with hepatitis and kidney injury; systemic glucocorticoids are recommended for moderate–severe organ involvement.
  • (D) Continue allopurinol and add an oral antihistamine — Continuing the culprit drug allows ongoing immune activation and organ damage. Antihistamines only help itch.
  • (E) Continue allopurinol at a lower dose — Dose reduction does not stop an immune reaction. Allopurinol must never be given again to this patient.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Timing separates the big drug eruptions: morbilliform exanthem 1–2 weeks, SJS/TEN 4–28 days (mucosal erosions, skin detachment), DRESS 2–8 weeks (eosinophilia, organs), AGEP within days (sterile pustules).

🎯 Educational objective

DRESS presents 2–8 weeks after drugs such as allopurinol with fever, rash, eosinophilia and organ injury; stop the drug and give systemic glucocorticoids with a slow taper when organs are involved.

EN-001.stem_html:
A 38-year-old woman comes to the office with 10 days of pain in the front of her neck that spreads to her jaw and ears. She also has palpitations, sweating and trouble sleeping. Three weeks ago she had a sore throat and cough that resolved on their own. She takes no medications.

Temperature is 37.9 °C (100.2 °F), blood pressure is 128/72 mm Hg and pulse is 108/min. The thyroid is mildly enlarged, firm and exquisitely tender to palpation. There is a fine tremor of the outstretched hands. There is no proptosis or lid lag.

TSH<0.01 µU/mL
Free T₄3.1 ng/dL
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate82 mm/h
Leukocyte count9,800/µL
24-hour radioactive iodine uptake1% (normal 10%–30%)
EN-001.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
EN-001.explain_html:
Correct answer: D Subacute (de Quervain) thyroiditis

A painful, tender thyroid after a viral illness, fever, a very high ESR, thyrotoxicosis and a near-zero radioiodine uptake is subacute granulomatous (de Quervain) thyroiditis.

The problem is leakage, not overproduction. Inflammation breaks follicles and releases stored hormone into the blood; the gland is not making new hormone, so uptake is low. The course has three phases: thyrotoxic (weeks) → hypothyroid (weeks–months) → recovery in most patients.

Treatment is supportive: a beta-blocker for adrenergic symptoms and an NSAID for pain. Use prednisone (for example 40 mg/day tapered over weeks) if pain is severe or does not respond to NSAIDs.

Low-uptake thyrotoxicosis Clue
Subacute thyroiditis Tender gland, fever, high ESR
Painless / postpartum thyroiditis Nontender, within 1 year of delivery, TPO antibodies
Exogenous thyroid hormone Low thyroglobulin, small gland
Iodine load (amiodarone, contrast) History

Why not the others

  • (A) Radioactive iodine ablation — Radioiodine is not taken up by an inflamed gland (uptake 1%) and the condition is self-limited.
  • (B) Methimazole — Thionamides block hormone synthesis. Here the gland is not synthesizing extra hormone, so methimazole does not help.
  • (C) Total thyroidectomy — Surgery has no role in a self-limited inflammatory condition.
  • (E) Levothyroxine — Levothyroxine may be needed later if the hypothyroid phase is symptomatic or persists, but it worsens the current thyrotoxic phase.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Thyroglobulin separates thyroiditis (high) from surreptitious levothyroxine use (low) — both have low uptake.

🎯 Educational objective

Subacute thyroiditis causes painful, low-uptake thyrotoxicosis from hormone leakage; treat with a beta-blocker and an NSAID (or glucocorticoids if severe), not antithyroid drugs or radioiodine.

EN-002.stem_html:
A 59-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus comes for follow-up. He had an anterior myocardial infarction 2 years ago. He takes metformin 1000 mg twice daily, aspirin, atorvastatin 80 mg, metoprolol succinate and lisinopril. He has gained 4 kg (8.8 lb) over the past year despite trying to diet. He has no symptoms of heart failure.

Blood pressure is 128/78 mm Hg and BMI is 33 kg/m². Examination is normal.

Hemoglobin A1c7.9%
Creatinine1.0 mg/dL (eGFR 82 mL/min/1.73 m²)
Urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio18 mg/g
Echocardiogram (1 year ago)LV ejection fraction 55%
EN-002.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate addition to his regimen?
EN-002.explain_html:
Correct answer: D Type 2 diabetes with cardiovascular disease

In type 2 diabetes with established ASCVD, add a drug with proven cardiovascular benefit — a GLP-1 receptor agonist or an SGLT2 inhibitor — regardless of A1c and independent of metformin. These drugs lower major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) by about 12%–26% in outcome trials.

For this patient a GLP-1 receptor agonist (semaglutide, dulaglutide, liraglutide) is the best fit: it reduces MACE, lowers A1c about 1%–1.5% and causes meaningful weight loss, which he needs. An SGLT2 inhibitor would be preferred first if he had heart failure or albuminuric CKD.

Comorbidity First add
ASCVD GLP-1 RA or SGLT2 inhibitor with proven benefit
Heart failure (any EF) SGLT2 inhibitor
CKD (eGFR ≥20, albuminuria) SGLT2 inhibitor; GLP-1 RA if needed
Obesity GLP-1 RA or dual GIP/GLP-1 RA (tirzepatide)

Why not the others

  • (A) Sitagliptin — DPP-4 inhibitors are weight-neutral and safe but showed no MACE reduction in outcome trials.
  • (B) Pioglitazone — Pioglitazone causes weight gain and fluid retention (heart-failure risk) and is not a first choice for cardiovascular risk reduction.
  • (C) Glipizide — Sulfonylureas lower glucose but cause hypoglycemia and weight gain and have no cardiovascular benefit.
  • (E) Insulin glargine — Basal insulin is not needed at an A1c of 7.9% and adds weight gain and hypoglycemia; GLP-1 RAs are preferred before insulin.
🧠 Mnemonic

"Hearts love GLP, pumps love SGLT." Atherosclerosis → GLP-1 RA or SGLT2i; heart failure or kidneys → SGLT2i.

🎓 ABIM pearl

GLP-1 RAs are contraindicated with a personal or family history of medullary thyroid cancer or MEN2. Hold them before procedures with deep sedation because of delayed gastric emptying.

🎯 Educational objective

For type 2 diabetes with ASCVD, add a GLP-1 receptor agonist or SGLT2 inhibitor with proven cardiovascular benefit; favor a GLP-1 RA when weight loss is also a goal.

A 46-year-old woman is evaluated for a high calcium level found on routine laboratory testing. She feels well. She has no history of kidney stones or fractures. She takes no medications or supplements other than a daily multivitamin.

Examination is normal.

Calcium11.0 mg/dL
Albumin4.2 g/dL
Phosphorus2.4 mg/dL
Parathyroid hormone (intact)94 pg/mL
25-Hydroxyvitamin D34 ng/mL
Creatinine0.8 mg/dL
24-hour urine calcium260 mg
DXA (lowest T-score)−1.6 at the distal radius
Renal ultrasoundno nephrolithiasis or nephrocalcinosis
EN-003.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.E: Observation with annual calcium and creatinine measurement

EN-003.explain_html:
Correct answer: B Primary hyperparathyroidism

High calcium with an inappropriately normal or high PTH means primary hyperparathyroidism (most often a single adenoma). A 24-hour urine calcium of 260 mg excludes familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia (FHH), which has very low urinary calcium.

Surgery cures the disease and is recommended for symptomatic patients and for asymptomatic patients who meet any of the criteria below. She is younger than 50, so she should have a parathyroidectomy even though she feels well — young patients face decades of bone and kidney damage.

Surgery for asymptomatic PHPT if any of:
Serum calcium >1 mg/dL above the upper limit of normal
Age <50
Osteoporosis (T-score ≤ −2.5 at spine, hip or distal radius) or vertebral fracture
eGFR <60 mL/min, nephrolithiasis or nephrocalcinosis, or urine calcium >250 mg/day (women) / >300 mg/day (men) with high stone risk

Why not the others

  • (A) Hydrochlorothiazide — Thiazides raise serum calcium by increasing distal tubular calcium reabsorption and would worsen hypercalcemia.
  • (C) Cinacalcet — Cinacalcet lowers serum calcium in patients who cannot or will not have surgery; it does not improve bone density or cure the disease.
  • (D) Alendronate — Bisphosphonates protect bone in patients who cannot have surgery, but they do not treat the cause; her bone density is not in the osteoporotic range.
  • (E) Observation with annual calcium and creatinine measurement — Observation is reasonable only when no surgical criterion is met. Her age alone is an indication.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Order imaging (sestamibi, 4D-CT or ultrasound) after deciding on surgery — to localize the gland for the surgeon, not to make the diagnosis.

🎯 Educational objective

Primary hyperparathyroidism is diagnosed biochemically; parathyroidectomy is indicated for asymptomatic patients who are younger than 50 or have marked hypercalcemia, osteoporosis, or kidney involvement.

EN-004.stem_html:
A 66-year-old woman comes for follow-up of osteoporosis. Five years ago a DXA scan showed a lumbar spine T-score of −2.6 and a total hip T-score of −2.2, and she started alendronate weekly. She has taken it consistently. She has never had a fracture and has not fallen. She does not smoke, drinks rarely, and takes no glucocorticoids. She walks daily and takes calcium in food and vitamin D 1000 units daily.

Height is unchanged from 5 years ago. Examination is normal.

DXA today — lumbar spine T-score−2.1
DXA today — total hip T-score−1.9
Calcium9.4 mg/dL
25-Hydroxyvitamin D36 ng/mL
Creatinine0.8 mg/dL
EN-004.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.C: Stop alendronate and repeat DXA in 2–3 years

EN-004.explain_html:
Correct answer: C Osteoporosis — bisphosphonate drug holiday

Bisphosphonates bind to bone and keep working for years after they are stopped. After 5 years of oral therapy (3 years of IV zoledronic acid), reassess fracture risk.

She is now at lower risk: no fractures, hip T-score above −2.5, no new risk factors. For such patients, a drug holiday of 2–3 years is recommended — it keeps most of the benefit and lowers the rare but serious risks of long-term use: atypical femoral fracture and osteonecrosis of the jaw. Restart therapy when bone density falls or a fracture occurs.

After 5 y oral / 3 y IV bisphosphonate Plan
Low risk (no fracture, hip T > −2.5) Drug holiday, reassess in 2–3 years
High risk (hip T ≤ −2.5, fracture before or on therapy) Continue up to 10 y oral / 6 y IV, or switch

Why not the others

  • (A) Add teriparatide to alendronate — Anabolic therapy is for very high risk (recent fracture, T ≤ −3.0, multiple fractures). Combining with a bisphosphonate is not standard.
  • (B) Switch to denosumab — Denosumab is a strong option for high-risk patients, but it has no lasting effect — once started, it should not be stopped without follow-up therapy. Not needed here.
  • (D) Continue alendronate for another 5 years — Ten years of therapy is for patients who stay at high risk. In low-risk patients, extended therapy adds little fracture benefit and more atypical femoral fractures.
  • (E) Switch to raloxifene — Raloxifene is weaker (vertebral only) and raises the risk of venous thromboembolism and hot flashes. No reason to switch.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Never take a holiday from denosumab. Stopping it causes rapid bone loss and rebound multiple vertebral fractures — always follow it with a bisphosphonate.

🎯 Educational objective

After 5 years of oral bisphosphonate therapy, offer a 2–3-year drug holiday to women at lower fracture risk (no fracture, hip T-score above −2.5); continue or switch therapy for those at high risk.

EN-005.stem_html:
A 74-year-old woman comes to the office because of 2 weeks of fatigue and mild unsteadiness. Six weeks ago hydrochlorothiazide was added to her amlodipine for hypertension. She drinks about 2 L of fluid per day. She has no vomiting, diarrhea, headache or confusion.

Blood pressure is 132/76 mm Hg without orthostatic change, and pulse is 76/min. Mucous membranes are moist, jugular venous pressure is normal, and there is no edema. She is alert and oriented, and neurologic examination is normal.

Sodium124 mEq/L (6 months ago 139 mEq/L)
Potassium3.3 mEq/L
Serum osmolality262 mOsm/kg H₂O
Glucose96 mg/dL
Creatinine0.8 mg/dL
Urine osmolality410 mOsm/kg H₂O
Urine sodium58 mEq/L
TSH1.8 µU/mL
Cortisol (8 AM)16 µg/dL
EN-005.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.B: Continue hydrochlorothiazide and restrict fluids to 1 L/day

EN-005.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Thiazide-induced hyponatremia

She has hypotonic hyponatremia (osmolality 262) with mild symptoms that began after starting a thiazide. Thiazides act in the distal convoluted tubule, where they impair the kidney's ability to make dilute urine while leaving the medullary concentrating gradient intact. Older women with low body mass are at highest risk, usually within the first weeks of therapy.

The fix is to stop the thiazide (and replace potassium). Sodium usually recovers over days to weeks. She should not be rechallenged with a thiazide — the problem tends to recur. A different antihypertensive class (for example an ACE inhibitor or ARB) can be used.

Correct slowly: limit the rise to ≤8 mEq/L in 24 hours in high-risk patients (hypokalemia, alcohol use, malnutrition, advanced liver disease) to avoid osmotic demyelination syndrome.

Why not the others

  • (B) Continue hydrochlorothiazide and restrict fluids to 1 L/day — Fluid restriction alone while continuing the offending drug leaves the cause in place.
  • (C) Intravenous 0.9% saline, 2 L over 12 hours — Isotonic saline helps hypovolemic hyponatremia; she is euvolemic, and with a urine osmolality of 410 the saline load can be partly excreted as concentrated urine, retaining free water.
  • (D) Start tolvaptan — Tolvaptan is for persistent euvolemic or hypervolemic hyponatremia when other measures fail; it risks overly rapid correction and liver injury, and the cause here is reversible.
  • (E) Intravenous 3% saline 100-mL bolus — Hypertonic saline boluses are for severe symptoms (seizures, obtundation, respiratory distress). She is alert with mild symptoms.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Hyponatremia + hypokalemia in an older woman = think thiazide first. Hypokalemia also accelerates sodium rise when K⁺ is replaced (K⁺ shifts into cells, Na⁺ out) — watch the overcorrection.

🎯 Educational objective

Thiazide-induced hyponatremia with mild symptoms is treated by stopping the thiazide, correcting potassium, and avoiding rapid sodium correction.

ET-001.stem_html:
A 58-year-old woman comes to the office with 1 week of brief spells of intense spinning. They happen when she rolls over in bed to the right, lies down, or tilts her head back to reach a high shelf, and each lasts less than a minute. She has mild nausea during spells but no hearing loss, tinnitus, ear fullness, headache, double vision, slurred speech or weakness. Between spells she feels normal.

Vital signs are normal. Hearing is grossly normal. With the patient turned to the right during the Dix–Hallpike maneuver, after a 5-second delay, she develops vertigo with upbeating, torsional nystagmus toward the right ear that fades after 20 seconds. Testing to the left is negative. The rest of the neurologic examination, including gait, is normal.
ET-001.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

choices.D: Vestibular rehabilitation exercises as the only treatment

ET-001.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo

Brief positional vertigo with a positive Dix–Hallpike — latency of a few seconds, upbeating torsional nystagmus, fatigable, lasting <1 minute — is benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV) of the right posterior semicircular canal. Loose otoconia (calcium carbonate crystals) drift into the canal and move with gravity when the head changes position.

Treat with a canalith repositioning maneuver (Epley) in the office. It moves the crystals back into the utricle and cures about 80% of patients after one to three maneuvers.

Positional nystagmus Peripheral (BPPV) Central (worrisome)
Latency Yes (2–20 s) None
Duration <1 min Persistent
Fatigability Yes No
Direction Upbeat-torsional (posterior canal) Pure vertical (often downbeat), changes direction
Other signs None Ataxia, diplopia, dysarthria

Why not the others

  • (B) Oral prednisone taper — Glucocorticoids may help acute vestibular neuritis (continuous vertigo for days), not positional vertigo.
  • (C) MRI of the brain — Classic BPPV with a typical Dix–Hallpike and normal neurologic examination does not need imaging.
  • (D) Vestibular rehabilitation exercises as the only treatment — Vestibular rehabilitation is an add-on for persistent imbalance; repositioning is the first-line cure.
  • (E) Meclizine daily for 4 weeks — Vestibular suppressants do not fix BPPV, delay central compensation and cause sedation and falls. Use them at most briefly for severe nausea.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Continuous vertigo for days with nystagmus at rest calls for HINTS (head impulse, nystagmus, test of skew) to separate vestibular neuritis from posterior circulation stroke.

🎯 Educational objective

Posterior-canal BPPV is diagnosed with the Dix–Hallpike maneuver and treated with canalith repositioning (Epley); avoid routine imaging and vestibular suppressants.

GE-001.stem_html:
A 78-year-old woman comes for an annual visit. She has fallen twice in the past year while walking in her home — once tripping on a rug, once turning quickly in the kitchen — without serious injury. She now worries about falling and walks less. She has hypertension treated with amlodipine and takes no sedatives or other medications. Her eyeglasses were updated 6 months ago.

Blood pressure is 132/74 mm Hg supine and 130/72 mm Hg standing, without symptoms. Corrected visual acuity is 20/30 in both eyes. She needs to push with her arms to rise from a chair. The Timed Up and Go test takes 16 seconds (normal <12 seconds) with a slow, cautious gait. Sensation and reflexes in the feet are normal.

25-Hydroxyvitamin D34 ng/mL
Hemoglobin13.1 g/dL
TSH2.2 µU/mL
GE-001.lead: Which of the following is the most effective intervention to reduce her risk of further falls?

choices.B: Advise her to limit walking to reduce exposure
choices.E: Exercise program with balance and strength training

GE-001.explain_html:
Correct answer: E Fall prevention

She screens positive for fall risk: two falls, fear of falling, slow Timed Up and Go and proximal leg weakness (needs arms to rise). Orthostatic hypotension, poor vision, medications and vitamin D deficiency are not the problem here.

The single best-proven intervention for community-dwelling older adults is exercise — especially programs that combine balance, gait and strength training (for example physical therapy, Otago, tai chi). Exercise reduces falls by about 20%–35%. Add a home safety assessment (rugs, lighting, grab bars).

Multifactorial assessment and intervention is also recommended for patients at high risk.

Why not the others

  • (A) Hip protectors — Hip protectors may reduce hip fractures in nursing-home residents with good adherence; they do not prevent falls.
  • (B) Advise her to limit walking to reduce exposure — Restricting activity worsens deconditioning and fear of falling and increases fall risk.
  • (C) Vitamin D 2000 units daily — In older adults without vitamin D deficiency, supplementation does not prevent falls (USPSTF recommends against it for this purpose).
  • (D) Stop amlodipine — Her blood pressure is well controlled without orthostatic drop; amlodipine is not contributing to her falls.
🧠 Mnemonic

Fall risk review — "I HATE FALLING": Inflammation of joints, Hypotension (orthostatic), Auditory/visual impairment, Tremor, Equilibrium problems, Foot problems, Arrhythmia, Leg-length mismatch, Lack of conditioning, Illness, Nutrition, Gait disturbance.

🎓 ABIM pearl

The "STEADI" approach: ask every patient ≥65 three questions — fallen in the past year? feel unsteady? worry about falling? A yes leads to gait, strength and balance testing.

🎯 Educational objective

Exercise programs with balance and strength training are the most effective intervention to prevent falls in community-dwelling older adults; vitamin D does not prevent falls in those without deficiency.

GE-002.stem_html:
An 82-year-old man is brought to the office by his daughter because he has been confused for 4 days. He has mild Alzheimer dementia and normally manages his own dressing and meals. Since earlier this week he has been drowsy during the day, awake and agitated at night, and at times does not recognize his grandson. Oxybutynin was started 6 days ago for urinary urgency. Other medications are donepezil and lisinopril.

Temperature is 37.0 °C (98.6 °F), blood pressure is 128/70 mm Hg and pulse is 84/min. He is inattentive and cannot name the months backward. Mucous membranes are dry. There is no focal neurologic deficit and no suprapubic tenderness; bladder scan shows 90 mL.

Glucosesodiumcalcium and creatinine
Complete blood countnormal
Urinalysisno leukocytes or nitrite
GE-002.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
GE-002.explain_html:
Correct answer: D Drug-induced delirium (anticholinergic)

Acute onset of fluctuating inattention and altered consciousness = delirium (superimposed on dementia). The timing points to a cause: oxybutynin, a strongly anticholinergic drug, started 2 days before symptoms. Anticholinergics cross the blood–brain barrier and directly worsen cognition — and they oppose donepezil.

The most effective treatment of delirium is to find and remove the cause. Stop oxybutynin; confusion usually clears over days. Use nondrug measures (reorientation, sleep hygiene, glasses and hearing aids, family presence). If urgency still needs treatment, try behavioral therapy or a β₃-agonist (mirabegron, vibegron) rather than another antimuscarinic.

  • (A) Noncontrast CT of the head — There is no trauma, focal deficit or anticoagulation, and a clear drug cause is present; imaging is low-yield.
  • (B) Lorazepam as needed for agitation — Benzodiazepines worsen delirium (except in alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal).
  • (C) Haloperidol at bedtime — Antipsychotics do not shorten delirium and add risks (falls, QT prolongation, higher mortality in dementia). Reserve them for severe agitation that endangers the patient.

Delirium in older adults is often drug-induced; stop strongly anticholinergic drugs such as oxybutynin and use nonpharmacologic measures rather than antipsychotics or benzodiazepines.

GI-001.stem_html:
A 58-year-old man comes to discuss the results of an upper endoscopy done for 10 years of frequent heartburn. He takes omeprazole 20 mg daily, which controls his symptoms well. He has no dysphagia, weight loss or bleeding. He is a former smoker.

Endoscopy showed salmon-colored mucosa extending 4 cm above the gastroesophageal junction without nodules or ulceration. Biopsies show intestinal metaplasia with goblet cells and no dysplasia, confirmed by a second gastrointestinal pathologist.
GI-001.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.A: Continue omeprazole and repeat endoscopy in 6 months
choices.B: Continue omeprazole and repeat endoscopy in 3 years
choices.D: Radiofrequency ablation of the Barrett segment
choices.E: Stop omeprazole because symptoms are controlled

GI-001.explain_html:
Correct answer: B Barrett esophagus without dysplasia

Barrett esophagus is columnar metaplasia of the distal esophagus (with goblet cells) caused by chronic acid reflux. It is the precursor of esophageal adenocarcinoma, but the risk without dysplasia is low — roughly 0.2%–0.5% per year.

For nondysplastic Barrett, management is:

  • Daily PPI (reduces inflammation; may lower progression).
  • Surveillance endoscopy with biopsies: every 3 years for segments ≥3 cm, every 5 years for segments <3 cm.

Ablation is reserved for dysplasia. The pathway escalates with the grade of dysplasia:

Biopsy Plan
No dysplasia, ≥3 cm PPI + EGD every 3 years
No dysplasia, <3 cm PPI + EGD every 5 years
Indefinite for dysplasia Optimize PPI, repeat EGD in 6 months
Low-grade dysplasia (confirmed) Endoscopic eradication therapy (or surveillance every 12 months)
High-grade dysplasia / intramucosal cancer Endoscopic resection of nodules + ablation

Why not the others

  • (A) Continue omeprazole and repeat endoscopy in 6 months — A 6-month interval is for "indefinite for dysplasia" after optimizing acid suppression, not for nondysplastic Barrett.
  • (C) Refer for esophagectomy — Esophagectomy is reserved for invasive cancer beyond the mucosa that cannot be treated endoscopically.
  • (D) Radiofrequency ablation of the Barrett segment — Ablation is for confirmed dysplasia; in nondysplastic Barrett, ablation risks (stricture, bleeding) outweigh the small benefit.
  • (E) Stop omeprazole because symptoms are controlled — Patients with Barrett esophagus should stay on a PPI even when symptoms are controlled.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Screening endoscopy for Barrett is suggested in patients with chronic GERD plus ≥3 risk factors: male sex, age >50, White race, central obesity, smoking, or a first-degree relative with Barrett or esophageal adenocarcinoma.

🎯 Educational objective

Nondysplastic Barrett esophagus is managed with a daily PPI and surveillance endoscopy every 3 years (segment ≥3 cm) or 5 years (segment <3 cm); ablation is for dysplasia.

GI-002.stem_html:
A 44-year-old woman was diagnosed with a duodenal ulcer 4 weeks ago when she presented with epigastric pain. Biopsies were positive for Helicobacter pylori. She completed 14 days of bismuth quadruple therapy (omeprazole, bismuth subsalicylate, tetracycline and metronidazole) 2 weeks ago. She is still taking omeprazole 40 mg daily and now has no pain.

Examination is normal. Hemoglobin is 12.9 g/dL.
GI-002.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate way to confirm eradication of H. pylori?

choices.A: Repeat upper endoscopy with biopsy now
choices.C: No testing is needed because her symptoms resolved
choices.E: Urea breath test at least 4 weeks after antibiotics, after holding omeprazole for 2 weeks

GI-002.explain_html:
Correct answer: E Helicobacter pylori — test of cure

Every patient treated for H. pylori should have a test of cure — resistance (especially to clarithromycin and metronidazole) makes treatment failure common, and symptom relief does not prove eradication.

Use a test of active infection: urea breath test, stool antigen, or biopsy-based tests. Two timing rules prevent false-negative results, because PPIs, bismuth and antibiotics suppress the bacteria without killing them:

  • At least 4 weeks after finishing antibiotics and bismuth.
  • PPI held for 1–2 weeks before testing (an H₂ blocker can cover symptoms).

Uncomplicated duodenal ulcer does not need repeat endoscopy. (Gastric ulcers are different — they often need repeat endoscopy to exclude cancer.)

Why not the others

  • (A) Repeat upper endoscopy with biopsy now — Endoscopy is not needed to confirm cure after an uncomplicated duodenal ulcer; a noninvasive test is preferred.
  • (B) Serum H. pylori IgG antibody now — Antibodies stay positive for months to years after cure, so serology cannot confirm eradication. It only proves past exposure.
  • (C) No testing is needed because her symptoms resolved — Symptom resolution does not mean the bacteria are gone; persistent infection risks recurrent ulcer and bleeding.
  • (D) Urea breath test now — Testing now is too soon after antibiotics and while on a PPI — both cause false-negative results.
🧠 Mnemonic

Test of cure "4 and 2": 4 weeks off antibiotics/bismuth, 2 weeks off PPI.

🎓 ABIM pearl

First-line therapy in the US is now bismuth quadruple therapy for 14 days when clarithromycin susceptibility is unknown. Vonoprazan-based dual or triple therapy is an alternative.

🎯 Educational objective

Confirm H. pylori eradication with a urea breath test, stool antigen or biopsy at least 4 weeks after antibiotics and 1–2 weeks after stopping PPIs; serology cannot confirm cure.

GI-003.stem_html:
A 38-year-old man comes to establish care. He feels well. His father was diagnosed with colorectal cancer at age 46 and is alive after surgery and chemotherapy. No other relatives have had cancer. The patient has no rectal bleeding, change in bowel habits or weight loss.

Examination is normal. Complete blood count is normal.
GI-003.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate colorectal cancer screening plan?

choices.A: Stool DNA–FIT test now and every 3 years
choices.B: Begin screening at age 45 with colonoscopy every 10 years
choices.C: Colonoscopy now and every 5 years if normal
choices.D: Begin screening at age 45 with annual fecal immunochemical testing
choices.E: CT colonography now and every 10 years

GI-003.explain_html:
Correct answer: C Colorectal cancer screening — family history

Average-risk adults begin screening at 45. Family history changes both when and how.

With one first-degree relative diagnosed before age 60 (or two at any age), screening is by colonoscopy, starting at age 40 or 10 years before the relative's age at diagnosis, whichever comes first, and repeated every 5 years. His father was 46 → start at 36. He is already 38, so the first colonoscopy is due now.

Family history Start Test & interval
None (average risk) 45 Colonoscopy q10y, FIT q1y, stool DNA–FIT q1–3y, CT colonography q5y, sigmoidoscopy q5y
1 FDR <60 y, or ≥2 FDRs any age 40 or 10 y before youngest diagnosis Colonoscopy q5y
1 FDR ≥60 y 40 Average-risk tests and intervals

Why not the others

  • (A) Stool DNA–FIT test now and every 3 years — Stool DNA–FIT is not recommended for screening people with a first-degree relative diagnosed young.
  • (B) Begin screening at age 45 with colonoscopy every 10 years — Starting at 45 is too late and the 10-year interval is too long for his risk.
  • (D) Begin screening at age 45 with annual fecal immunochemical testing — Age 45 and annual FIT are for average-risk adults. His family history moves him to colonoscopy, starting earlier.
  • (E) CT colonography now and every 10 years — CT colonography is an average-risk option. In higher-risk patients, colonoscopy is preferred because it allows biopsy and polypectomy.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Ask whether the relative's tumor was tested for mismatch repair deficiency. A deficient tumor raises concern for Lynch syndrome, which needs genetic counseling and colonoscopy every 1–2 years starting at age 20–25.

🎯 Educational objective

A first-degree relative with colorectal cancer before age 60 calls for colonoscopy every 5 years starting at age 40 or 10 years before the relative's diagnosis, whichever is earlier.

GI-004.topic: Cirrhosis — primary prophylaxis of variceal bleeding
GI-004.stem_html:
A 57-year-old man with alcohol-associated cirrhosis comes for follow-up. He has not had alcohol for 18 months. He has never had ascites, encephalopathy or gastrointestinal bleeding. Screening upper endoscopy last week showed large esophageal varices without red wale signs or stigmata of recent bleeding.

Blood pressure is 122/74 mm Hg and pulse is 82/min. There is mild splenomegaly and no ascites.

Platelets88,000/µL
Albumin3.7 g/dL
Bilirubintotal1.2 mg/dL
INR1.2
Creatinine0.9 mg/dL
GI-004.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment to prevent variceal bleeding?

choices.A: No treatment; repeat endoscopy in 1 year

GI-004.explain_html:
Correct answer: E Cirrhosis — primary prophylaxis of variceal bleeding

Large varices that have never bled need primary prophylaxis. The options are a nonselective beta-blocker (NSBB) or endoscopic band ligation. NSBBs are now preferred in compensated cirrhosis because they also lower the risk of first decompensation (ascites), not just bleeding.

Carvedilol is the NSBB of choice: it blocks β₁ (lowers cardiac output), β₂ (unopposed α-constriction of splanchnic vessels → less portal inflow) and α₁ (lowers intrahepatic resistance). It lowers portal pressure more than propranolol. Typical dose 6.25 mg daily, increasing to 12.5 mg daily as tolerated.

Stop or reduce NSBBs if systolic BP falls below 90 mm Hg, or with refractory ascites plus hypotension, AKI or spontaneous bacterial peritonitis.

Why not the others

  • (A) No treatment; repeat endoscopy in 1 year — Large varices carry a high bleeding risk (mortality ~15%–20% per bleed); waiting without treatment is not appropriate.
  • (B) Transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS) — TIPS is for bleeding that cannot be controlled or recurs despite therapy, and for refractory ascites — not for primary prophylaxis.
  • (C) Isosorbide mononitrate — Nitrates alone do not prevent variceal bleeding and can worsen hypotension and renal perfusion.
  • (D) Metoprolol — Metoprolol is β₁-selective. It lacks the β₂ effect that reduces splanchnic flow, so it does not lower portal pressure enough.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Patients who cannot take a beta-blocker get band ligation every 2–8 weeks until varices are eradicated. Once on carvedilol, no repeat endoscopy is needed to "check" the varices.

🎯 Educational objective

Prevent the first variceal bleed in cirrhosis with large varices with a nonselective beta-blocker — carvedilol is preferred — or band ligation if beta-blockers cannot be used.

GI-005.stem_html:
A 48-year-old woman was admitted 3 days ago with severe epigastric pain radiating to the back and vomiting. Lipase was 2,400 U/L. She received intravenous lactated Ringer solution and analgesics. Today she is hungry, her pain is gone, and she is eating a low-fat diet without discomfort. She drinks alcohol rarely.

Temperature is 37.0 °C (98.6 °F), blood pressure is 124/78 mm Hg and pulse is 80/min. The abdomen is soft with mild epigastric tenderness.

Admission ALT312 U/L
Today ALT96 U/L
Today bilirubintotal0.9 mg/dL
Triglycerides140 mg/dL
Calcium9.1 mg/dL
Right upper quadrant ultrasoundmultiple gallstones; common bile duct 5 mm; no pericholecystic fluid
GI-005.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.A: Start imipenem to prevent infected necrosis
choices.C: Discharge home and arrange elective cholecystectomy in 6–8 weeks

GI-005.explain_html:
Correct answer: E Gallstone pancreatitis

This is mild acute biliary pancreatitis: gallstones, an early transaminase spike (ALT >150 U/L in the first 48 hours strongly suggests a gallstone cause), and normal triglycerides and calcium. A stone passed through the ampulla and caused pancreatitis.

The key decision is timing of cholecystectomy. After mild gallstone pancreatitis, cholecystectomy during the same admission cuts the risk of recurrent biliary events — up to about 1 in 5 patients have another episode (pancreatitis, cholecystitis, colic) while waiting weeks for surgery.

Severe necrotizing pancreatitis is the exception: surgery is delayed until collections resolve or mature (usually >6 weeks).

Why not the others

  • (A) Start imipenem to prevent infected necrosis — Prophylactic antibiotics do not prevent infected necrosis and are not recommended in acute pancreatitis.
  • (B) Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) before discharge — ERCP is for cholangitis or persistent biliary obstruction. Her bilirubin is normal and the duct is not dilated, so the stone has passed.
  • (C) Discharge home and arrange elective cholecystectomy in 6–8 weeks — Delaying cholecystectomy in mild disease leaves a high early risk of recurrent pancreatitis and other gallstone complications.
  • (D) Start ursodeoxycholic acid and discharge — Ursodiol dissolves stones slowly and incompletely and does not prevent recurrent pancreatitis; it is for patients who cannot have surgery.
🎓 ABIM pearl

HE-001.topic: Iron deficiency anemia in an older man
HE-001.stem_html:
A 67-year-old man comes to the office because of 3 months of fatigue and shortness of breath when climbing stairs. He has no abdominal pain, change in bowel habits, black stools, hematochezia, hematuria or weight loss. He eats meat several times a week. He takes aspirin 81 mg daily for primary prevention. His last colonoscopy was 12 years ago and was normal.

Pulse is 92/min. The conjunctivae are pale. Abdominal examination is normal. Rectal examination shows brown stool.

Hemoglobin10.1 g/dL
Mean corpuscular volume74 fL
RDW17.8%
Platelets410,000/µL
Ferritin8 ng/mL
Transferrin saturation6%
Tissue transglutaminase IgA (with normal total IgA)negative
HE-001.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.B: Oral iron and recheck hemoglobin in 3 months

HE-001.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Iron deficiency anemia in an older man

A ferritin of 8 ng/mL confirms iron deficiency (ferritin <45 ng/mL is the AGA threshold in anemic patients). In a man or a postmenopausal woman, iron deficiency anemia is gastrointestinal blood loss — possibly from cancer — until proven otherwise.

The evaluation is bidirectional endoscopy (colonoscopy + upper endoscopy), which finds a cause in a large share of patients; colorectal cancer, gastric cancer, peptic ulcer disease and angioectasias are leading causes. Celiac disease (iron malabsorption) should also be tested — done here.

Replace iron too — but iron is not a substitute for finding the source.

Iron studies Iron deficiency Anemia of inflammation
Ferritin Low Normal or high
Transferrin saturation Low Low–normal
TIBC High Low

Why not the others

  • (B) Oral iron and recheck hemoglobin in 3 months — Treating with iron alone may mask an occult GI cancer. Endoscopic evaluation is required.
  • (C) Bone marrow biopsy — Iron studies already explain the anemia; marrow examination is not needed.
  • (D) Capsule endoscopy — Capsule endoscopy evaluates the small bowel after a negative bidirectional endoscopy.
  • (E) Fecal immunochemical test — A negative stool test does not exclude a GI cause because bleeding is intermittent; it has no role in evaluating established iron deficiency anemia.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Platelets are often mildly high in iron deficiency (reactive thrombocytosis) — it does not point to a myeloproliferative neoplasm.

🎯 Educational objective

Iron deficiency anemia in men and postmenopausal women requires bidirectional endoscopy (and celiac testing) to find a gastrointestinal source, especially cancer.

HE-002.stem_html:
A 54-year-old man comes for follow-up 6 weeks after a proximal deep venous thrombosis of the left femoral vein. It was diagnosed 3 weeks after an elective left total knee arthroplasty, while he was still using crutches. He has been taking apixaban without bleeding. He now walks normally and has returned to work. He has no history of venous thromboembolism or cancer, and age-appropriate cancer screening is up to date.

The left calf is minimally swollen and nontender.
HE-002.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate duration of anticoagulation?
HE-002.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Provoked deep venous thrombosis — duration

This DVT was provoked by a major transient risk factor — surgery (and immobility) — which has now resolved. The risk of recurrence after stopping anticoagulation is low (about 1% per year), lower than the bleeding risk of continuing.

Treat a provoked proximal DVT or PE for 3 months, then stop. Longer or indefinite therapy is for unprovoked VTE (low bleeding risk), persistent risk factors (active cancer, antiphospholipid syndrome) or recurrent VTE.

VTE type Duration
Provoked by surgery or major transient factor 3 months
Provoked by minor transient factor (estrogen, travel, minor injury) 3 months (consider longer case by case)
Unprovoked, low–moderate bleeding risk Extended (indefinite), reassess yearly; reduced-dose DOAC is an option after 6 months
Active cancer Extended while cancer is active

Why not the others

  • (B) Indefinite — Indefinite therapy is for unprovoked or recurrent VTE or persistent risk factors.
  • (C) 12 months — Twelve months adds bleeding risk without meaningful benefit for a surgically provoked clot.
  • (D) 6 weeks — Six weeks is too short for a proximal DVT; it raises recurrence risk. (Isolated distal DVT has different rules.)
  • (E) Decide after a thrombophilia panel — Thrombophilia testing does not change management after a clearly provoked first VTE and is not recommended.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Do not test for thrombophilia while the patient is acutely ill or on anticoagulants — heparin lowers antithrombin, warfarin lowers proteins C and S, and DOACs interfere with clotting-based assays.

🎯 Educational objective

Treat a first proximal DVT or PE provoked by surgery for 3 months, then stop; reserve extended therapy for unprovoked VTE or persistent risk factors.

ID-001.stem_html:
A 32-year-old man comes to the office with 3 days of fever, productive cough and right-sided pleuritic chest pain. He has no medical problems, takes no medications and has not taken antibiotics in the past year. He has no drug allergies. He does not smoke or drink alcohol heavily.

Temperature is 38.6 °C (101.5 °F), blood pressure is 124/76 mm Hg, pulse is 98/min, respirations are 20/min and oxygen saturation is 97% on room air. Crackles and bronchial breath sounds are heard at the right base. He is alert and drinking fluids well.

Chest radiograph shows right lower lobe consolidation. Blood urea nitrogen is 12 mg/dL.
ID-001.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

choices.E: Hospital admission for intravenous ceftriaxone and azithromycin

ID-001.explain_html:
Correct answer: C Community-acquired pneumonia — outpatient

He has community-acquired pneumonia with CURB-65 = 0 (no confusion, BUN <20, RR <30, BP normal, age <65) → treat at home.

For an outpatient without comorbidities or MRSA/Pseudomonas risk factors, ATS/IDSA recommends high-dose amoxicillin (1 g three times daily), which covers Streptococcus pneumoniae, the most common and most lethal bacterial cause. Doxycycline is an alternative. A macrolide alone is used only where pneumococcal macrolide resistance is <25%, which is not true in most of the US.

Outpatient CAP Regimen (5 days minimum, until stable)
No comorbidities Amoxicillin 1 g TID, or doxycycline, or macrolide (if local resistance <25%)
Comorbidities (heart, lung, liver, kidney disease, diabetes, alcohol use disorder, cancer, asplenia) Amoxicillin–clavulanate or a cephalosporin plus macrolide or doxycycline, or a respiratory fluoroquinolone alone

Why not the others

  • (A) Azithromycin — Macrolide monotherapy fails against resistant pneumococci; US resistance rates are well above 25%.
  • (B) Levofloxacin — Respiratory fluoroquinolones are reserved for patients with comorbidities or beta-lactam allergy because of tendon rupture, aortic aneurysm, QT prolongation, C. difficile and resistance concerns.
  • (D) Amoxicillin–clavulanate plus azithromycin — Combination therapy is for outpatients with comorbidities. He has none.
  • (E) Hospital admission for intravenous ceftriaxone and azithromycin — CURB-65 of 0 and normal oxygenation support outpatient care.
🧠 Mnemonic

CURB-65: Confusion, Urea (BUN) >19 mg/dL, Respiratory rate ≥30, BP <90 systolic or ≤60 diastolic, age ≥65. 0–1 → home; 2 → consider admission; ≥3 → hospital, think ICU.

🎓 ABIM pearl

Treat for at least 5 days and until afebrile for 48–72 hours with stable vital signs. A follow-up chest film is not routinely needed if he recovers.

🎯 Educational objective

Treat outpatient community-acquired pneumonia in a healthy adult without risk factors with high-dose amoxicillin (or doxycycline); reserve fluoroquinolones and combination therapy for patients with comorbidities.

ID-002.stem_html:
A 27-year-old woman comes to the office with 2 days of painful urination, urgency and frequency. She has no fever, chills, flank pain, vaginal discharge or itching. Her last menstrual period was 2 weeks ago and a urine pregnancy test is negative. She had one similar episode 3 years ago. She has no drug allergies.

Temperature is 36.9 °C (98.4 °F). There is mild suprapubic tenderness and no costovertebral angle tenderness.

Urine dipstick is positive for leukocyte esterase and nitrite.
ID-002.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

choices.A: No antibiotic until urine culture results are available

ID-002.explain_html:
Correct answer: E Acute uncomplicated cystitis

Dysuria and frequency without vaginal symptoms in a nonpregnant woman has a >90% probability of acute uncomplicated cystitis. No culture is needed before treatment for a typical first or infrequent episode.

First-line choices (IDSA) are agents with low resistance and little collateral damage to gut flora:

First-line Course
Nitrofurantoin monohydrate/macrocrystals 100 mg BID 5 days
Trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole DS BID 3 days (if local resistance <20%)
Fosfomycin 3 g single dose
Pivmecillinam 3–5 days

Nitrofurantoin reaches high concentrations only in urine, so do not use it for pyelonephritis or when creatinine clearance is very low.

Why not the others

  • (A) No antibiotic until urine culture results are available — Waiting for culture delays relief. Cultures are for recurrent, complicated or atypical cases, or suspected pyelonephritis.
  • (B) Amoxicillin for 7 days — E. coli resistance to amoxicillin is high; aminopenicillins alone are not recommended for empiric cystitis therapy.
  • (C) Ciprofloxacin for 3 days — Fluoroquinolones work but are reserved for pyelonephritis or when first-line agents cannot be used, because of serious adverse effects and resistance.
  • (D) Ceftriaxone intramuscularly once — Parenteral ceftriaxone is unnecessary for lower-tract infection in an outpatient who can take oral medication.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Fever, flank pain or CVA tenderness → pyelonephritis: get a urine culture and use a fluoroquinolone or TMP-SMX (if susceptible), often after one IV dose of ceftriaxone.

🎯 Educational objective

Treat acute uncomplicated cystitis empirically with nitrofurantoin for 5 days (or TMP-SMX, fosfomycin, or pivmecillinam); reserve fluoroquinolones for pyelonephritis.

ID-003.stem_html:
A 52-year-old man comes for a routine health visit. He feels well. He has no chronic medical conditions, does not smoke and takes no medications. He received a tetanus–diphtheria–pertussis (Tdap) vaccine 5 years ago and an influenza vaccine this fall. He has never received a pneumococcal vaccine.

Examination is normal.
ID-003.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate pneumococcal vaccination for this patient?

choices.B: PPSV23 now and PCV20 in 1 year
choices.C: A single dose of 20-valent pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV20) now
choices.E: 15-valent pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV15) now and no further doses

ID-003.explain_html:
Correct answer: C Adult pneumococcal vaccination

Since late 2024, CDC recommends pneumococcal vaccination for all adults aged 50 years and older (and for younger adults with risk conditions), regardless of health.

For adults who have never received a conjugate vaccine, give one dose of PCV20 or PCV21 — that completes the series. Alternatively, give PCV15 followed by PPSV23 one year later.

Conjugate vaccines link the polysaccharide to a protein carrier, which recruits T-cell help and produces memory and better immunogenicity than plain polysaccharide vaccines.

Why not the others

  • (A) 23-valent pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine (PPSV23) now — PPSV23 alone is no longer recommended as the first or only vaccine; it gives weaker, shorter immunity than conjugate vaccines.
  • (B) PPSV23 now and PCV20 in 1 year — Starting with PPSV23 is the outdated sequence; when both are needed, the conjugate vaccine goes first.
  • (D) No pneumococcal vaccine until age 65 — The age threshold for routine vaccination was lowered from 65 to 50 years.
  • (E) 15-valent pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV15) now and no further doses — PCV15 must be followed by PPSV23 (usually ≥1 year later) to complete the series.
🧠 Mnemonic

"Twenty at fifty" — PCV20 (or PCV21) once at 50+ and you are done.

🎓 ABIM pearl

He is also due for recombinant zoster vaccine (2 doses, 2–6 months apart) — recommended for all adults ≥50, even with a prior shingles episode.

🎯 Educational objective

All adults aged 50 years or older who have not received a pneumococcal conjugate vaccine should get a single dose of PCV20 or PCV21 (or PCV15 followed by PPSV23).

ID-004.stem_html:
A 68-year-old man is scheduled for extraction of a fractured molar next week. Four years ago he had a bioprosthetic aortic valve replacement for aortic stenosis. He has hypertension and takes lisinopril and aspirin. He has no drug allergies and no history of endocarditis.

Examination shows a soft systolic ejection murmur at the right upper sternal border. Echocardiography 6 months ago showed a normally functioning prosthetic valve.
ID-004.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation before the procedure?

choices.A: Amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily for 7 days after the procedure
choices.B: Clindamycin 600 mg orally before the procedure
choices.C: Amoxicillin 2 g orally 30–60 minutes before the procedure

ID-004.explain_html:
Correct answer: C Infective endocarditis prophylaxis

Antibiotic prophylaxis before dental work is now limited to patients at highest risk of a bad outcome from endocarditis, and only for procedures that manipulate the gingiva or periapical region or perforate the oral mucosa (extractions qualify).

Prosthetic valves of any type (including bioprosthetic and transcatheter valves, and valve repairs with prosthetic material) are a highest-risk condition. The regimen is a single dose of amoxicillin 2 g orally 30–60 minutes before the procedure.

Prosthetic valve or prosthetic material used in valve repair
Previous infective endocarditis
Unrepaired cyanotic congenital heart disease; repaired CHD with residual shunt or defect near prosthetic material
Cardiac transplant with valvulopathy

Why not the others

  • (A) Amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily for 7 days after the procedure — Prophylaxis is a single dose before the procedure; a postprocedure course adds adverse effects without benefit.
  • (B) Clindamycin 600 mg orally before the procedure — Clindamycin is no longer recommended for penicillin-allergic patients because it causes more C. difficile infection; azithromycin, clarithromycin or doxycycline are used instead.
  • (D) Intravenous vancomycin before the procedure — IV vancomycin is unnecessary for an outpatient dental procedure in a patient without penicillin allergy.
  • (E) No antibiotic prophylaxis — A prosthetic valve is one of the few conditions where prophylaxis is still recommended.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Prophylaxis is not recommended for GI or GU procedures (colonoscopy, cystoscopy) in any of these patients, or for mitral valve prolapse, bicuspid aortic valve or native valve regurgitation alone. Good oral hygiene prevents far more endocarditis than antibiotics.

🎯 Educational objective

Give a single preprocedure dose of amoxicillin 2 g before dental procedures involving the gingiva in patients with prosthetic valves, prior endocarditis, or certain congenital heart disease.
