ID-005.stem_html:
A 45-year-old woman comes to the office with 2 days of a painful, red, swollen area on her left lower leg. She has no injury, recent travel or prolonged immobility. She has hypertension. She has no drug allergies.

Temperature is 37.7 °C (99.9 °F), blood pressure is 132/80 mm Hg and pulse is 88/min. There is a 10 × 8 cm warm, tender, poorly demarcated area of erythema on the anterior shin with no fluctuance, drainage, crepitus or bullae. Point-of-care ultrasound shows subcutaneous edema without a fluid collection. Scaling and maceration are present between the toes of the left foot.
ID-005.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
ID-005.explain_html:
Correct answer: D Nonpurulent cellulitis

This is nonpurulent cellulitis — spreading erythema, warmth and tenderness without pus or an abscess. The usual cause is beta-hemolytic streptococci (group A and others) entering through broken skin — here interdigital tinea pedis.

Treat mild nonpurulent cellulitis with an oral agent active against streptococci: cephalexin, dicloxacillin, penicillin V or amoxicillin, typically for 5–6 days, extended if not improving. Elevate the leg — it speeds resolution.

Nonpurulent (cellulitis/erysipelas) Purulent (abscess, furuncle)
Main organism Streptococci S. aureus (often MRSA)
Key treatment Beta-lactam (cephalexin) Incision and drainage ± TMP-SMX or doxycycline

Why not the others

  • (A) Incision and drainage — There is no abscess to drain on examination or ultrasound.
  • (B) Trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole — TMP-SMX has unreliable activity against streptococci; it is used for purulent infections where MRSA is likely.
  • (C) Hospital admission for intravenous vancomycin — She has no systemic toxicity, hypotension or rapidly spreading infection. IV therapy and MRSA coverage are for moderate–severe or purulent infection.
  • (E) Topical mupirocin — Topical antibiotics treat impetigo; they do not reach dermal and subcutaneous infection.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Prevent recurrence by treating tinea pedis, edema and venous insufficiency. Bilateral "cellulitis" is almost always something else — usually stasis dermatitis.

🎯 Educational objective

Treat mild nonpurulent cellulitis with an oral antistreptococcal beta-lactam such as cephalexin; reserve MRSA-active drugs for purulent infections and drainage for abscesses.

MS-001.stem_html:
A randomized controlled trial enrolls 8,000 adults with atrial fibrillation who cannot take anticoagulants. Patients are assigned to a new drug or placebo and followed for 5 years. The primary outcome is stroke.

Group Patients Strokes at 5 years
New drug 4,000 240 (6%)
Placebo 4,000 400 (10%)
MS-001.lead: How many patients must be treated with the new drug for 5 years to prevent one stroke?
MS-001.explain_html:
Correct answer: C Number needed to treat

Number needed to treat (NNT) = 1 ÷ absolute risk reduction (ARR).

  • Control event rate (CER) = 10% = 0.10
  • Experimental event rate (EER) = 6% = 0.06
  • ARR = CER − EER = 0.10 − 0.06 = 0.04
  • NNT = 1 / 0.04 = 25

Treating 25 patients for 5 years prevents one stroke. The relative risk reduction (RRR) is (0.10 − 0.06) / 0.10 = 40% — a bigger-sounding number that hides how often the event happens.

Measure Formula Here
Absolute risk reduction CER − EER 4%
Relative risk EER / CER 0.6
Relative risk reduction 1 − RR 40%
NNT 1 / ARR 25

Why not the others

  • (A) 4 — "4" confuses the ARR (4%) with the NNT.
  • (B) 10 — "10" is the placebo event rate expressed as a percentage, not the NNT.
  • (D) 40 — "40" is the relative risk reduction (40%), not the NNT.
  • (E) 60 — "60" reflects the relative risk (0.6) and is not an NNT.
🧠 Mnemonic

"Absolutely flip it" — NNT is the reciprocal of the absolute (not relative) risk reduction. Always round up to the next whole patient.

🎓 ABIM pearl

The same formula gives the number needed to harm (NNH): 1 ÷ absolute risk increase of an adverse event. Compare NNT with NNH when weighing a therapy.

🎯 Educational objective

Number needed to treat equals 1 divided by the absolute risk reduction; relative risk reduction overstates benefit when baseline risk is low.

NE-001.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate first step in management?
NE-001.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Hyperkalemia with ECG changes

The strip shows tall, peaked T waves, flattened P waves and a widened QRS — hyperkalemia with ECG changes, a medical emergency that can deteriorate to sine-wave rhythm, ventricular fibrillation or asystole without warning.

Treat in three steps, and the first is always to protect the heart:

Step Drugs Onset
1. Stabilize the membrane IV calcium gluconate 3 g (or calcium chloride 1 g via central line); repeat if ECG unchanged 1–3 min, lasts 30–60 min
2. Shift K⁺ into cells Regular insulin 10 units IV + dextrose (if glucose <250); nebulized albuterol 10–20 mg 15–30 min
3. Remove K⁺ from the body Loop diuretic (if making urine), potassium binder (SZC, patiromer), dialysis if refractory or anuric Hours

Calcium does not lower potassium — it restores the gap between resting and threshold potential so the heart cannot fire chaotically. Then stop spironolactone and lisinopril and look for the cause.

Why not the others

  • (B) Intravenous furosemide — Loop diuretics help remove potassium if he is making urine, but they act slowly and do not protect the heart.
  • (C) Intravenous regular insulin with dextrose — Insulin–dextrose is essential and comes right after calcium; it lowers potassium in 15–30 minutes but does not protect the myocardium immediately.
  • (D) Emergency hemodialysis — Dialysis is the definitive removal therapy for refractory hyperkalemia or kidney failure; it comes after membrane stabilization and shifting.
  • (E) Sodium zirconium cyclosilicate orally — Binders take hours to work and are for potassium removal after stabilization.
🧠 Mnemonic

"C-BIG-K-Drop": Calcium, Beta-agonist, Insulin + Glucose, Kayexalate/binders, Diuretics/dialysis.

🎓 ABIM pearl

In patients on digoxin with hyperkalemia, calcium is still given when ECG changes are present; the "stone heart" fear is not supported by modern data.

🎯 Educational objective

Hyperkalemia with ECG changes is treated first with intravenous calcium to stabilize the cardiac membrane, then insulin–dextrose and albuterol to shift potassium, and finally measures to remove potassium.

NE-002.stem_html:
A 44-year-old man comes to the office after passing his third calcium oxalate kidney stone in 4 years. To prevent stones he has stopped eating dairy products. He drinks about 1.2 L of fluid daily and eats fast food several times a week. He has hypertension and takes no medications.

Blood pressure is 142/88 mm Hg. Examination is normal.

Calcium (serum)9.6 mg/dL
Parathyroid hormone38 pg/mL
Uric acid (serum)5.8 mg/dL
24-hour urine — volume1.3 L
24-hour urine — calcium340 mg (normal <300 mg)
24-hour urine — oxalate38 mg (normal <45 mg)
24-hour urine — citrate620 mg (normal >450 mg)
24-hour urine — sodium230 mEq
24-hour urine — uric acid610 mg (normal <800 mg)
NE-002.lead: In addition to increasing fluid intake, which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation?

choices.C: Start chlorthalidone and reduce dietary sodium

NE-002.explain_html:
Correct answer: C Recurrent calcium nephrolithiasis

His 24-hour urine shows idiopathic hypercalciuria (normal serum calcium and PTH) with low urine volume and high sodium intake — the drivers of his calcium stones.

The plan:

  • Fluids to make >2.5 L of urine per day (the single most effective measure).
  • Thiazide diuretic (chlorthalidone, indapamide or hydrochlorothiazide): increases distal calcium reabsorption → lowers urine calcium and stone recurrence. It also treats his hypertension.
  • Low sodium diet: sodium drags calcium into urine; a high-salt diet blunts the thiazide effect.
  • Normal dietary calcium (1000–1200 mg/day) and moderate animal protein.

Why not the others

  • (A) Start potassium citrate — Potassium citrate is for hypocitraturia (or uric acid stones). His citrate is normal; it is also an add-on to offset thiazide-induced hypokalemia.
  • (B) Start vitamin C 1000 mg daily — Vitamin C is metabolized to oxalate and increases calcium oxalate stone risk.
  • (D) Start allopurinol — Allopurinol is for calcium stones with hyperuricosuria (and normal urine calcium) or for uric acid stones. His urine uric acid is normal.
  • (E) Continue avoiding dairy products — A low-calcium diet increases stones: less calcium in the gut leaves more free oxalate to be absorbed, raising urine oxalate. It also harms bone.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Every first stone needs serum calcium and a stone analysis; recurrent stones (or a first stone in a high-risk patient) need a 24-hour urine to pick targeted therapy.

🎯 Educational objective

Recurrent calcium stones with idiopathic hypercalciuria are prevented with high fluid intake, a thiazide diuretic, sodium restriction and a normal-calcium diet.

A 66-year-old man is evaluated in the emergency department after a 40-minute episode of weakness of the right hand and slurred speech that began while he was reading. Symptoms resolved completely 2 hours ago. He has hypertension and type 2 diabetes. He takes lisinopril and metformin.

Blood pressure is 158/88 mm Hg and pulse is 76/min, regular. Neurologic examination is normal (NIH Stroke Scale score 0).

Noncontrast head CTno hemorrhage or acute infarct
MRI brain with diffusion-weighted imagingno infarct
CT angiography of head and neck30% stenosis of the left internal carotid artery; no large-vessel occlusion
ECG and 24-hour telemetrysinus rhythm
LDL cholesterol132 mg/dL
NR-001.lead: In addition to a high-intensity statin, which of the following is the most appropriate antithrombotic therapy?

choices.B: Aspirin plus clopidogrel for 21 days, then a single antiplatelet agent

NR-001.explain_html:
Correct answer: B High-risk transient ischemic attack

He had a high-risk TIA: motor weakness and speech disturbance lasting >10 minutes. His ABCD² score is 6 (age ≥60 = 1, BP ≥140/90 = 1, unilateral weakness = 2, duration 10–59 min = 1, diabetes = 1). The 90-day stroke risk is highest in the first 48 hours.

For high-risk TIA (ABCD² ≥4) or minor ischemic stroke (NIHSS ≤3) without a cardioembolic source, dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin + clopidogrel) started within 24 hours and continued for 21 days, then a single agent, lowers early recurrent stroke (CHANCE, POINT). Longer DAPT adds bleeding without further benefit.

ABCD² Points
Age ≥60 1
BP ≥140/90 at evaluation 1
Clinical: unilateral weakness 2; speech disturbance without weakness 1 1–2
Duration: ≥60 min 2; 10–59 min 1 1–2
Diabetes 1

Why not the others

  • (A) Apixaban — Anticoagulation is for cardioembolic sources such as atrial fibrillation; telemetry showed sinus rhythm. Prolonged monitoring for AF is still reasonable.
  • (C) Intravenous alteplase — Thrombolysis is for a disabling deficit present at treatment; his symptoms resolved.
  • (D) Aspirin alone — Aspirin alone is appropriate for low-risk TIA or after the 21-day DAPT period, but it is less effective early after a high-risk TIA.
  • (E) Aspirin plus clopidogrel indefinitely — Long-term DAPT increases major bleeding without additional stroke prevention.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Symptomatic carotid stenosis 70%–99% (and selected 50%–69%) on the side of symptoms → carotid endarterectomy within 2 weeks. His 30% stenosis does not qualify.

🎯 Educational objective

After a high-risk TIA or minor ischemic stroke, start aspirin plus clopidogrel within 24 hours for 21 days, then continue single antiplatelet therapy with a high-intensity statin.

NR-002.stem_html:
A 34-year-old woman comes to the office because of migraines. She has had migraine without aura since her teens, but over the past year attacks have become more frequent — now about 8 headache days per month — and she has missed work several times. Sumatriptan usually relieves an attack within 2 hours; she uses it 6–8 days a month. She also has hypertension, diagnosed 6 months ago and not yet treated. She uses a copper IUD.

Blood pressure is 142/90 mm Hg on two readings and pulse is 82/min. Neurologic examination, including fundoscopy, is normal.
NR-002.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate preventive treatment?
NR-002.explain_html:
Correct answer: E Migraine prevention

She needs migraine prevention: ≥4 headache days per month with disability (many experts use ≥4 days, or fewer if attacks are severe or acute drugs fail or are overused).

First-line oral preventives include propranolol or metoprolol, topiramate, amitriptyline, venlafaxine and candesartan. Choose by comorbidity: her hypertension makes a β-blocker the natural choice — one drug, two problems. Start low, titrate, and judge benefit after 2–3 months. CGRP-targeting therapies (monoclonal antibodies, gepants) are also accepted first-line options, and are especially useful when oral preventives fail or cause side effects.

Comorbidity Good preventive choice Avoid
Hypertension Propranolol, metoprolol, candesartan —
Depression, insomnia Amitriptyline, venlafaxine —
Obesity Topiramate Amitriptyline, valproate
Asthma Topiramate, candesartan β-blockers
Possible pregnancy — Valproate, topiramate (teratogenic)

Why not the others

  • (A) Verapamil plus daily ibuprofen — Verapamil has weak evidence for migraine, and daily NSAID use (≥15 days a month) causes medication-overuse headache.
  • (B) Butalbital–acetaminophen–caffeine as needed — Butalbital combinations cause medication-overuse headache and dependence and are not recommended for migraine.
  • (C) Daily sumatriptan — Using a triptan ≥10 days a month causes medication-overuse headache; daily use is never a preventive strategy.
  • (D) Oxycodone as needed — Opioids worsen migraine over time, cause medication-overuse headache and carry addiction risk.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Combined hormonal contraception is contraindicated in migraine with aura (stroke risk). She has migraine without aura, but her untreated hypertension would also argue against estrogen.

🎯 Educational objective

Offer migraine prevention for frequent or disabling migraine, selecting the agent by comorbidity (a β-blocker for coexisting hypertension), and avoid frequent acute-drug use that leads to medication-overuse headache.

OB-001.stem_html:
A 31-year-old woman comes for a routine health visit. Her last cervical cytology (Pap test) was 3 years ago at age 28 and was normal; she has never had an abnormal result. She received the HPV vaccine series as a teenager. She has one male partner and has never been diagnosed with HIV infection or another immunocompromising condition.

Examination, including pelvic examination, is normal.
OB-001.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate cervical cancer screening?

choices.C: High-risk HPV testing now, and every 5 years if negative
choices.D: No screening because she completed HPV vaccination
choices.E: Cervical cytology now and every year

OB-001.explain_html:
Correct answer: C Cervical cancer screening

At 30–65 years, average-risk women can be screened with any of three strategies (USPSTF):

Age Strategy
21–29 Cytology every 3 years
30–65 High-risk HPV (hrHPV) testing alone every 5 years, or cotesting (hrHPV + cytology) every 5 years, or cytology alone every 3 years
>65 Stop if adequate negative prior screening and no CIN2+ in the past 25 years

She is due now (3 years since normal cytology). Primary hrHPV testing finds more precancer than cytology and allows a 5-year interval after a negative result. Many guidelines (ACS, ACOG) now prefer it, and self-collected HPV samples are an accepted option.

Why not the others

  • (A) Cytology now and every 10 years — Cytology alone needs a 3-year interval.
  • (B) Colposcopy — Colposcopy is for abnormal screening results, not routine screening.
  • (D) No screening because she completed HPV vaccination — Vaccination does not cover all oncogenic HPV types; vaccinated women follow the same screening schedule.
  • (E) Cervical cytology now and every year — Annual screening finds no more cancers than 3- or 5-year intervals, and it causes more false positives and unnecessary procedures.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Women with HIV, organ transplant, DES exposure or prior CIN2+ need more frequent screening, and screening continues past 65 for them.

🎯 Educational objective

For average-risk women aged 30–65, screen with primary high-risk HPV testing every 5 years (or cotesting every 5 years, or cytology every 3 years).

OB-002.stem_html:
A 29-year-old woman comes to the office to discuss contraception. She wants to avoid pregnancy for at least 3–4 years. She has migraine with aura — about twice a month she sees zigzag lines for 20 minutes before the headache begins. She does not smoke. She has no history of venous thromboembolism or hypertension. She asks about "the pill" because a friend uses it.

Blood pressure is 116/72 mm Hg. BMI is 24 kg/m². Examination is normal. Urine pregnancy test is negative.
OB-002.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate contraceptive method?

choices.A: Combined oral contraceptive taken continuously without placebo week
choices.C: Combined oral contraceptive with 20 µg ethinyl estradiol

OB-002.explain_html:
Correct answer: B Contraception in migraine with aura

Migraine with aura is a US MEC category 4 condition for combined (estrogen-containing) hormonal contraception — an unacceptable health risk at any age. Estrogen and migraine with aura each raise the risk of ischemic stroke, and together the risk multiplies.

Progestin-only and nonhormonal methods are safe (category 1–2). For someone wanting reliable long-term contraception, a long-acting reversible contraceptive (LARC) — levonorgestrel IUD, copper IUD or etonogestrel implant — is the most effective choice (failure <1% per year). The levonorgestrel IUD also reduces menstrual bleeding and cramping.

Estrogen-containing methods are category 4 with:
Migraine with aura
Age ≥35 and smoking ≥15 cigarettes/day
Current or past VTE (not on anticoagulation), known thrombophilia
BP ≥160/100, vascular disease, complicated valvular disease
Breast cancer (current), decompensated cirrhosis, hepatocellular tumors
<21 days postpartum

Why not the others

  • (A) Combined oral contraceptive taken continuously without placebo week — Continuous use of a combined pill still exposes her to estrogen; it is contraindicated with aura.
  • (C) Combined oral contraceptive with 20 µg ethinyl estradiol — Any estrogen dose, even 20 µg, is contraindicated with migraine with aura because of stroke risk.
  • (D) Contraceptive vaginal ring (etonogestrel–ethinyl estradiol) — The vaginal ring contains ethinyl estradiol and carries the same contraindication.
  • (E) Transdermal contraceptive patch — The patch delivers estrogen (with higher overall exposure than many pills) — also contraindicated.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Migraine without aura is category 2 for combined methods if age <35 (category 3 if ≥35 when starting). The single most important question in a migraine patient wanting the pill: "Do you get an aura?"

🎯 Educational objective

Estrogen-containing contraception is contraindicated in migraine with aura; offer a progestin-only or nonhormonal method, preferably a long-acting reversible contraceptive.

ON-001.stem_html:
A 42-year-old woman comes for a routine health visit. She feels well and has no breast symptoms. She has never had a mammogram. Menarche was at age 13 and she had her first child at 29. She has no history of chest radiation or breast biopsy. Her maternal aunt had breast cancer at age 68; no other relatives have had breast, ovarian, pancreatic or prostate cancer.

Breast examination is normal.
ON-001.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate breast cancer screening recommendation?

choices.C: Genetic testing for BRCA1 and BRCA2
choices.E: Clinical breast examination alone every year

ON-001.explain_html:
Correct answer: B Breast cancer screening

She is at average risk: no personal history of breast cancer or chest radiation, no known high-risk mutation, and only a second-degree relative diagnosed after menopause.

The USPSTF (2024) recommends biennial screening mammography for all women aged 40–74. Starting at 40 rather than 50 was adopted because breast cancer rates in women in their 40s are rising and screening in this decade prevents deaths — with the most benefit for Black women, who have higher breast cancer mortality.

Risk group Screening
Average risk Mammography every 2 years, ages 40–74 (many groups also accept annual)
Lifetime risk ≥20%, BRCA carrier, chest radiation age 10–30 Annual mammography plus annual MRI, often starting at 25–30
Dense breasts Mammography; evidence for supplemental imaging is insufficient

Why not the others

  • (A) Annual breast MRI starting now — Breast MRI is for high-risk women (lifetime risk ≥20%, known mutation, chest radiation), not average-risk screening.
  • (C) Genetic testing for BRCA1 and BRCA2 — A single second-degree relative with postmenopausal breast cancer does not meet criteria for genetic testing.
  • (D) Begin mammography at age 50 — Starting at 50 is the older (2016) recommendation; screening now begins at 40.
  • (E) Clinical breast examination alone every year — Clinical breast examination alone is not a substitute for mammography.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Use a familial risk tool (for example, the USPSTF-recommended BRCA risk tools) when a family history includes breast cancer before 50, ovarian cancer, male breast cancer, multiple relatives, or Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry.

🎯 Educational objective

Average-risk women should have screening mammography every 2 years from age 40 to 74.

ON-002.stem_html:
A 58-year-old man comes for a routine health visit. He smoked 1 pack of cigarettes per day from age 24 to age 49 (25 pack-years) and quit 9 years ago. He feels well, has no cough, hemoptysis or weight loss, and is active. He has hypertension controlled with lisinopril.

Examination is normal.
ON-002.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate lung cancer screening recommendation?

choices.A: Annual low-dose CT of the chest
choices.B: No screening because he quit smoking more than 5 years ago
choices.D: A single low-dose CT of the chest now

ON-002.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Lung cancer screening

The USPSTF (2021) recommends annual low-dose CT (LDCT) for adults who:

  • are 50–80 years old,
  • have ≥20 pack-years of smoking, and
  • currently smoke or quit within the past 15 years.

He meets all three (58 years, 25 pack-years, quit 9 years ago). LDCT screening reduced lung cancer mortality by 20% in NLST and about 24% in NELSON. Screening stops when the person has not smoked for 15 years, develops a condition that limits life expectancy, or would not want or be fit for curative surgery.

Start with shared decision-making about benefits, false positives, overdiagnosis and radiation.

Why not the others

  • (B) No screening because he quit smoking more than 5 years ago — The cutoff is 15 years since quitting, not 5.
  • (C) Annual chest radiography — Chest radiography does not reduce lung cancer mortality and is not a screening test.
  • (D) A single low-dose CT of the chest now — Screening is annual; a single scan gives much less benefit.
  • (E) Sputum cytology every year — Sputum cytology misses most early cancers and is not recommended.
🧠 Mnemonic

"50-20-15" — age 50–80, 20 pack-years, quit within 15 years.

🎓 ABIM pearl

The American Cancer Society (2023) no longer uses the years-since-quitting limit — it recommends screening former smokers with ≥20 pack-years regardless of quit date. Payers usually follow USPSTF.

🎯 Educational objective

Screen adults aged 50–80 with ≥20 pack-years who smoke or quit within 15 years with annual low-dose CT.

ON-003.stem_html:
A 68-year-old man with metastatic prostate cancer to bone comes to the emergency department with 2 weeks of worsening mid-back pain that is worse lying down and wakes him at night. Since yesterday his legs feel heavy and he stumbled twice. He has not had urinary retention or incontinence.

Vital signs are normal. There is tenderness over the T9–T10 spinous processes. Strength is 4/5 in hip flexors and knee extensors bilaterally. Pinprick sensation is reduced below the umbilicus. Knee reflexes are brisk and plantar responses are extensor.
ON-003.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.A: Intravenous dexamethasone and emergency MRI of the entire spine
choices.C: Plain radiographs of the thoracic spine
choices.D: Oral oxycodone and outpatient MRI within 1 week

ON-003.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Malignant spinal cord compression

New back pain in a patient with cancer, worse lying down, plus leg weakness, a sensory level (T10 = umbilicus) and upper motor neuron signs = metastatic epidural spinal cord compression — an oncologic emergency. Function at the time of treatment predicts function afterward: patients who walk into treatment usually keep walking.

Steps, without delay:

  1. Dexamethasone IV (commonly 10 mg load, then 4 mg every 6 hours) to reduce vasogenic edema — give it as soon as the diagnosis is suspected in a patient with deficits.
  2. Emergency MRI of the entire spine with and without contrast — metastases are often at more than one level.
  3. Definitive therapy within hours: surgical decompression + radiation for selected patients (single-level compression, instability, good prognosis), otherwise radiation therapy.

Why not the others

  • (B) Lumbar puncture — Lumbar puncture does not diagnose cord compression and can worsen herniation of a compressed cord.
  • (C) Plain radiographs of the thoracic spine — Radiographs miss epidural disease and delay MRI.
  • (D) Oral oxycodone and outpatient MRI within 1 week — Neurologic deficits make this an emergency; waiting a week risks permanent paralysis.
  • (E) Whole-body bone scan — A bone scan shows bone metastases but not the epidural space or cord.
🧠 Mnemonic

Cancers that most often compress the cord — "Lung, Breast, Prostate" (each ~15%–20%), then renal cell, lymphoma and myeloma.

🎓 ABIM pearl

Thoracic spine is the most common level (~60%). Back pain that worsens when lying flat or with Valsalva in a cancer patient deserves an MRI even before deficits appear.

🎯 Educational objective

Suspected malignant spinal cord compression with neurologic deficits requires immediate dexamethasone, emergency whole-spine MRI and urgent radiation or surgery.

OP-001.stem_html:
A 66-year-old woman comes to the emergency department 2 hours after the sudden onset of severe pain in her right eye, blurred vision, halos around lights, frontal headache, nausea and vomiting. Symptoms began while she was watching a movie in a dark theater. She is farsighted. She took an over-the-counter cold remedy containing diphenhydramine this morning.

Visual acuity is counting fingers in the right eye and 20/25 in the left. The right eye shows conjunctival injection most intense around the cornea, a hazy cornea and a mid-dilated pupil that reacts poorly to light. The right globe feels hard on gentle palpation.
OP-001.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.A: Dilate the pupil with tropicamide to examine the fundus
choices.D: Topical ocular hypotensive drops and acetazolamide, with emergency ophthalmology evaluation
choices.E: Topical prednisolone acetate and follow-up with ophthalmology in 1 week

OP-001.explain_html:
Correct answer: D Acute angle-closure glaucoma

This is acute angle-closure glaucoma — an emergency that can cause permanent vision loss within hours. In a predisposed eye (farsighted, shallow anterior chamber, older age), pupillary dilation (darkness, anticholinergic or sympathomimetic drugs) pushes the iris against the trabecular meshwork. Aqueous humor cannot drain and intraocular pressure rises sharply (often >40–50 mm Hg).

Treat immediately to lower pressure, then fix the anatomy:

  • Aqueous suppressants: topical timolol, an α₂-agonist (apraclonidine/brimonidine), and acetazolamide 500 mg IV or orally.
  • Pilocarpine (miotic) once pressure starts falling, to pull the iris away from the angle.
  • Hyperosmotic agents (IV mannitol) if pressure remains very high.
  • Emergency ophthalmology for laser peripheral iridotomy — the definitive treatment — and usually prophylactic iridotomy of the other eye.

Why not the others

  • (A) Dilate the pupil with tropicamide to examine the fundus — Dilating the pupil worsens angle closure — the cause of this attack.
  • (B) Topical moxifloxacin — Antibiotic drops treat bacterial conjunctivitis or keratitis; vision loss, a hard eye and a fixed pupil are not infection.
  • (C) Noncontrast CT of the head — Head imaging delays sight-saving treatment; the eye findings explain the headache and vomiting.
  • (E) Topical prednisolone acetate and follow-up with ophthalmology in 1 week — Glucocorticoid drops treat inflammation (for example anterior uveitis) but do not lower the pressure, and a 1-week delay risks blindness.
🧠 Mnemonic

Red-eye red flags — "VIP-PC": Vision loss, Intense pain, Photophobia, Pupil abnormal, Corneal haze. Any one → same-day ophthalmology.

🎓 ABIM pearl

The headache and vomiting can mimic migraine, subarachnoid hemorrhage or an abdominal process — always look at the eye in an older adult with sudden headache and nausea.

🎯 Educational objective

Acute angle-closure glaucoma presents with a painful red eye, halos, a cloudy cornea and a mid-dilated fixed pupil; lower intraocular pressure immediately and arrange emergency laser iridotomy.

PS-001.stem_html:
A 45-year-old man comes to the office because he wants help to stop drinking. He drinks 8–10 beers daily and has failed to cut down several times. He finished a supervised outpatient withdrawal 1 week ago and has not had a drink since. He has opioid use disorder in remission and has taken buprenorphine–naloxone daily for 3 years. He attends weekly counseling.

Vital signs are normal. There is no tremor, jaundice or stigmata of chronic liver disease.

ALT48 U/L
AST66 U/L
Bilirubintotal0.8 mg/dL
Albumin4.1 g/dL
Creatinine0.9 mg/dL (eGFR >90 mL/min/1.73 m²)
PS-001.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate medication to help him maintain abstinence from alcohol?
PS-001.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Alcohol use disorder — pharmacotherapy

Medications for alcohol use disorder (AUD) are underused even though they reduce relapse. The two first-line drugs are naltrexone and acamprosate; the choice depends on the patient.

He takes buprenorphine, an opioid. Naltrexone is an opioid antagonist — it would block buprenorphine's effect and can precipitate opioid withdrawal, risking relapse to opioid use. Acamprosate (a glutamate modulator that eases protracted withdrawal) has no opioid interaction and is cleared by the kidneys, not the liver — a good fit for him.

Drug Best when Avoid when
Naltrexone (oral or monthly IM) Reducing heavy drinking; craving Any opioid use, acute hepatitis or liver failure
Acamprosate Maintaining abstinence after withdrawal; liver disease CrCl ≤30; reduce dose CrCl 30–50
Disulfiram Highly motivated, supervised dosing Heart disease, psychosis, poor adherence
Gabapentin, topiramate Second line —

Why not the others

  • (B) Naltrexone — Naltrexone is contraindicated with ongoing opioid therapy such as buprenorphine.
  • (C) No medication; counseling alone — Combining medication with counseling works better than counseling alone; he should be offered pharmacotherapy.
  • (D) Disulfiram — Disulfiram works only with supervised adherence and has weaker evidence; it is not first-line.
  • (E) Diazepam daily — Benzodiazepines treat acute withdrawal; long-term use is addictive and dangerous with alcohol and buprenorphine (respiratory depression).
🎓 ABIM pearl

Mild aminotransferase elevation (AST > ALT, as here) is not a reason to avoid naltrexone in other patients — the risk is in acute hepatitis or decompensated cirrhosis.

🎯 Educational objective

Offer naltrexone or acamprosate to patients with alcohol use disorder; choose acamprosate when the patient takes opioids (including buprenorphine) and avoid it in severe kidney disease.

PS-002.stem_html:
A 31-year-old woman comes to the office because she "can't turn her brain off." For the past 8 months she has worried almost every day about her job, finances and her parents' health, even when things are going well. She feels restless and tense, has trouble concentrating, tires easily and lies awake worrying. She has no panic attacks, no thoughts of self-harm and no prior psychiatric treatment. She drinks one glass of wine on weekends and does not use other substances. She does not plan pregnancy and uses an IUD.

Vital signs and examination are normal. Her GAD-7 score is 15 (moderate–severe). PHQ-9 score is 6.

TSH1.6 µU/mL
Complete blood count and metabolic panelnormal
PS-002.lead: In addition to referral for cognitive behavioral therapy, which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

choices.D: Hydroxyzine nightly as the only medication

PS-002.explain_html:
Correct answer: E Generalized anxiety disorder

Excessive, hard-to-control worry about many things on most days for ≥6 months, with restlessness, fatigue, poor concentration, muscle tension and insomnia, is generalized anxiety disorder (GAD). Hyperthyroidism and substances are excluded.

First-line treatment is cognitive behavioral therapy and/or an SSRI or SNRI (sertraline, escitalopram, venlafaxine XR, duloxetine). Start at a low dose (anxious patients feel early activation side effects), increase after 1–2 weeks, and allow 4–6 weeks for effect. Continue for 6–12 months after response before tapering.

Why not the others

  • (A) Alprazolam as needed — Benzodiazepines relieve anxiety quickly but cause dependence, tolerance, falls and cognitive effects, and do not treat co-occurring depression; they are at most a short-term bridge, never first-line.
  • (B) Propranolol — Propranolol blunts physical symptoms of performance anxiety but does not treat GAD.
  • (C) Quetiapine — Atypical antipsychotics have some efficacy but cause weight gain, metabolic syndrome and other adverse effects; they are not first-line.
  • (D) Hydroxyzine nightly as the only medication — Hydroxyzine is a second-line option with sedation and anticholinergic effects; on its own it is not the preferred first treatment.
🧠 Mnemonic

GAD — "Worried WARRIORS": Worry, Anxious, Restless, Reduced concentration, Irritability, On edge/muscle tension, Rest disturbed (sleep), Six months.

🎓 ABIM pearl

Screen all adults for anxiety (USPSTF 2023 recommends screening adults <65 years) and always ask about suicidal thoughts when starting an antidepressant in young adults.

🎯 Educational objective

Treat generalized anxiety disorder with CBT and/or an SSRI or SNRI; avoid benzodiazepines as first-line therapy.

PU-001.stem_html:
A 67-year-old man with COPD comes for follow-up. He quit smoking 3 years ago after 45 pack-years. He uses tiotropium once daily and albuterol as needed; his inhaler technique is good. He gets short of breath walking about 100 meters on level ground. In the past year he had two exacerbations treated with oral prednisone and antibiotics, without hospitalization. He completed pulmonary rehabilitation last year.

Oxygen saturation is 94% on room air. There are scattered expiratory wheezes and a prolonged expiratory phase.

Post-bronchodilator FEV₁/FVC0.52
Post-bronchodilator FEV₁48% of predicted
Blood eosinophil count340/µL
PU-001.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate change to his maintenance therapy?

choices.A: Switch to a long-acting β₂-agonist–long-acting muscarinic antagonist–inhaled glucocorticoid (triple) inhaler
choices.E: Add an inhaled glucocorticoid alone to tiotropium

PU-001.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Stable COPD — escalating inhaled therapy

He has COPD with persistent dyspnea and ≥2 moderate exacerbations a year despite a LAMA. GOLD escalation depends on the blood eosinophil count, a marker of who benefits from inhaled glucocorticoids:

On LAMA or LABA, still exacerbating Escalate to
Eosinophils <100/µL LABA + LAMA
Eosinophils ≥300/µL (or ≥100 on LABA+LAMA) LABA + LAMA + ICS (single inhaler)
Still exacerbating on triple Add roflumilast (FEV₁ <50% + chronic bronchitis) or azithromycin (former smokers); consider dupilumab/mepolizumab if eosinophils ≥300

With eosinophils of 340/µL, triple therapy reduces exacerbations and, in trials, all-cause mortality compared with dual bronchodilators.

Why not the others

  • (B) Add daily oral prednisone 5 mg — Chronic systemic glucocorticoids cause serious harm (osteoporosis, diabetes, myopathy, infection) without benefit in stable COPD.
  • (C) Add roflumilast — Roflumilast is a later add-on for patients who still exacerbate on triple therapy, with FEV₁ <50% and chronic bronchitis.
  • (D) Add daily azithromycin — Azithromycin is also a later add-on after triple therapy (best in former smokers); it can prolong QT and cause hearing loss and resistance.
  • (E) Add an inhaled glucocorticoid alone to tiotropium — ICS should be given with a LABA, not as LAMA + ICS alone. ICS without a LABA is not a recommended COPD combination.
🎓 ABIM pearl

ICS raises pneumonia risk. Avoid or withdraw ICS when eosinophils are <100/µL, with repeated pneumonia, or with mycobacterial infection.

🎯 Educational objective

In COPD with exacerbations despite a long-acting bronchodilator, escalate to triple therapy (LABA + LAMA + ICS) when blood eosinophils are ≥300/µL, and to LABA + LAMA when they are low.

PU-002.stem_html:
A 26-year-old woman comes to the office because she uses her albuterol inhaler 2–3 times per week for cough, chest tightness and wheezing, especially with exercise and in cold air. She has not woken at night because of asthma and has never needed oral glucocorticoids or emergency care. She has allergic rhinitis.

Examination is normal.

SpirometryFEV₁ 88% of predicted; FEV₁/FVC 0.74
After bronchodilatorFEV₁ increases by 15% (420 mL)
PU-002.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
PU-002.explain_html:
Correct answer: E Mild asthma

She has mild asthma (symptoms less than daily, no night waking, normal FEV₁, a significant bronchodilator response).

The biggest change in asthma care: SABA-only treatment is no longer recommended. Even mild asthma carries a risk of severe and fatal attacks, and SABA alone does nothing for airway inflammation. As-needed low-dose ICS–formoterol (budesonide–formoterol) gives anti-inflammatory therapy every time she treats symptoms; it cuts severe exacerbations by about 60% compared with SABA alone, using far less steroid than daily ICS. Formoterol works within minutes, so it works as a reliever.

(Daily low-dose ICS with a SABA reliever is an acceptable alternative pathway.)

Why not the others

  • (A) Oral prednisone for 5 days — She is not having an exacerbation. Systemic glucocorticoids are for acute attacks.
  • (B) Salmeterol twice daily — LABA without ICS increases asthma-related deaths. Never give salmeterol alone in asthma.
  • (C) Montelukast daily — Leukotriene receptor antagonists are less effective than ICS and carry an FDA boxed warning for neuropsychiatric effects.
  • (D) Continue albuterol as needed only — SABA monotherapy increases the risk of severe exacerbations and death and is no longer recommended at any step.
🧠 Mnemonic

"Every puff gets a steroid." In asthma, the reliever should carry ICS.

🎓 ABIM pearl

Before stepping up any asthma therapy, check inhaler technique, adherence, triggers (smoke, allergens, NSAIDs, β-blockers) and comorbidities (rhinitis, GERD, obesity, OSA).

🎯 Educational objective

Treat mild asthma with as-needed low-dose ICS–formoterol (or daily low-dose ICS); SABA-only therapy and LABA monotherapy are not recommended.

PU-003.stem_html:
A 52-year-old woman had a CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis in the emergency department for right flank pain, which showed a 4-mm obstructing ureteral stone that later passed. The lung bases on the scan showed a 7-mm solid nodule with smooth margins in the right lower lobe. She has never smoked, has no history of cancer and no known exposures to asbestos or radon. She feels well and has no cough, hemoptysis or weight loss.

Examination is normal. There is no prior chest imaging.
PU-003.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

choices.B: CT of the chest in 6–12 months
choices.E: CT of the chest in 3 months

PU-003.explain_html:
Correct answer: B Incidental pulmonary nodule

The Fleischner Society guidelines apply to incidental nodules in adults ≥35 years (not to lung cancer screening, known cancer or immunosuppression). Management depends on size, type (solid vs subsolid) and patient risk.

For a single solid nodule 6–8 mm in a low-risk patient (never-smoker, no other risk factors, smooth margins), get a CT at 6–12 months, then consider another at 18–24 months. A solid nodule that is unchanged for 2 years is considered benign.

Single solid nodule Low risk High risk
<6 mm No routine follow-up Optional CT at 12 months
6–8 mm CT at 6–12 months, then consider 18–24 months CT at 6–12 months and 18–24 months
>8 mm CT at 3 months, PET-CT or tissue sampling Same

Why not the others

  • (A) PET-CT now — PET-CT is unreliable below about 8 mm (false negatives) and is reserved for larger solid nodules.
  • (C) CT-guided needle biopsy — Biopsy of a 7-mm low-risk nodule is high-risk and low-yield.
  • (D) No further follow-up — "No follow-up" applies to nodules <6 mm in low-risk patients.
  • (E) CT of the chest in 3 months — A 3-month CT is for nodules >8 mm.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Subsolid (ground-glass) nodules grow slowly — follow them longer (up to 5 years). A growing solid component is the most worrisome change.

🎯 Educational objective

A single incidental 6–8-mm solid lung nodule in a low-risk patient needs a follow-up chest CT at 6–12 months (Fleischner Society).

PU-004.stem_html:
A 50-year-old man comes to discuss the results of a sleep study. His wife reports loud snoring and pauses in his breathing. He falls asleep while watching television and once nodded off at a red light. He has hypertension treated with amlodipine and lisinopril. He drinks 1–2 beers on weekends and takes no sedatives.

Blood pressure is 146/90 mm Hg. BMI is 34 kg/m² and neck circumference is 45 cm (17.7 in). The oropharynx is crowded.

A home sleep apnea test shows an apnea–hypopnea index of 32 events/hour with oxygen saturation nadir of 81%.
PU-004.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
PU-004.explain_html:
Correct answer: E Obstructive sleep apnea

He has severe obstructive sleep apnea (AHI ≥30) with excessive daytime sleepiness — including drowsy driving — and hypertension.

CPAP is first-line therapy for moderate–severe OSA. It splints the upper airway open, abolishes apneas, improves sleepiness and quality of life, lowers motor-vehicle crash risk and modestly lowers blood pressure. Success depends on adherence (≥4 hours per night): mask fitting, humidification and early follow-up matter.

Weight loss is recommended for everyone with OSA and obesity; GLP-1-based therapy can reduce AHI in obesity-related OSA and can be added to, not substituted for, CPAP when sleepiness is dangerous.

AHI (events/h) Severity
5–14 Mild
15–29 Moderate
≥30 Severe

Why not the others

  • (A) Zolpidem at bedtime — Sedative-hypnotics can worsen apneas and oxygen desaturation.
  • (B) Mandibular advancement oral appliance — Oral appliances are an option for mild–moderate OSA or for patients who cannot tolerate CPAP; they are less effective in severe OSA.
  • (C) Modafinil — Modafinil treats residual sleepiness in patients already adherent to CPAP; it does not treat apneas or hypoxemia.
  • (D) Uvulopalatopharyngoplasty — Upper-airway surgery has modest, unpredictable success and is reserved for selected patients who fail or cannot use CPAP.
🧠 Mnemonic

STOP-BANG screen: Snoring, Tired, Observed apneas, Pressure (hypertension), BMI >35, Age >50, Neck >40 cm, Gender male. ≥5 = high risk.

🎓 ABIM pearl

Use in-lab polysomnography rather than a home test when the patient has significant cardiopulmonary disease, neuromuscular weakness, chronic opioid use, prior stroke or suspected hypoventilation.

🎯 Educational objective

CPAP is first-line treatment for moderate–severe obstructive sleep apnea, especially with daytime sleepiness; oral appliances are for mild–moderate disease or CPAP intolerance.

RH-001.stem_html:
A 66-year-old man comes to the office with 1 day of severe pain, redness and swelling of his right first metatarsophalangeal joint. He had two similar episodes last year. Allopurinol 100 mg daily was started 4 months ago and increased to 200 mg daily 6 weeks ago. He also has hypertension and chronic kidney disease. Medications are allopurinol, amlodipine and losartan. He stopped taking the colchicine prescribed with allopurinol after 2 months.

Temperature is 37.4 °C (99.3 °F). The right first MTP joint is red, warm, swollen and too tender to touch. No tophi are seen.

Creatinine1.8 mg/dL (eGFR 38 mL/min/1.73 m²)
Serum urate7.4 mg/dL
Leukocyte count9,600/µL
RH-001.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.A: Continue allopurinol and start oral prednisone for a short course
choices.B: Increase allopurinol to 600 mg daily as the only change
choices.C: Stop allopurinol until the flare resolves; start indomethacin
choices.D: Stop allopurinol and switch to febuxostat

RH-001.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Gout flare during urate-lowering therapy

Flares are common in the first months of urate-lowering therapy (ULT) — falling urate levels mobilize crystals from tissue deposits. That is a reason to keep ULT going, treat the flare, and use prophylaxis.

Treat the flare with any of the three anti-inflammatory options, choosing by comorbidities. With CKD stage 3b, NSAIDs are a poor choice, so a short oral glucocorticoid course (prednisone 30–40 mg/day, then taper over 7–10 days) is best. Low-dose colchicine is an alternative with renal dose adjustment and no interacting drugs.

Then:

  • Restart prophylaxis (low-dose colchicine or low-dose prednisone) for 3–6 months after starting ULT.
  • Titrate allopurinol upward every few weeks — even in CKD — to a serum urate <6 mg/dL.

Why not the others

  • (B) Increase allopurinol to 600 mg daily as the only change — Allopurinol should be titrated, but raising the dose does not treat the current flare.
  • (C) Stop allopurinol until the flare resolves; start indomethacin — Stopping ULT during a flare is unnecessary and causes urate swings that prolong flares; NSAIDs are also risky with CKD.
  • (D) Stop allopurinol and switch to febuxostat — Febuxostat is no more effective here and carries a boxed warning for cardiovascular death; the problem is the flare and an unmet urate target, not allopurinol failure.
  • (E) Continue allopurinol and start indomethacin — Continuing allopurinol is correct, but NSAIDs such as indomethacin can worsen kidney function with an eGFR of 38.
🧠 Mnemonic

"Start low, go slow, aim below 6" — allopurinol 100 mg (50 mg in CKD), increase by 100 mg every 2–5 weeks, target urate <6.

🎓 ABIM pearl

Before allopurinol, test for HLA-B*58:01 in patients of Southeast Asian (Han Chinese, Korean, Thai) or African American ancestry — carriers have a high risk of severe cutaneous reactions (SJS/TEN, DRESS).

🎯 Educational objective

Continue urate-lowering therapy during a gout flare, treat the flare according to comorbidities (glucocorticoids when NSAIDs are unsafe), add prophylaxis, and titrate to a serum urate below 6 mg/dL.

A 42-year-old woman comes to the office with 3 months of pain and swelling in both hands and wrists. Her hands are stiff for about 90 minutes every morning. She has trouble opening jars and typing at work. Ibuprofen helps partly. She does not plan pregnancy and uses a levonorgestrel IUD.

There is symmetric swelling and tenderness of the 2nd and 3rd metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints of both hands and both wrists. The distal interphalangeal joints are spared. There are no rashes, nail changes or nodules.

Rheumatoid factorpositive (high titer)
Anti–cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodiespositive (high titer)
C-reactive protein2.4 mg/dL
Complete blood countnormal
ALT18 U/L
Creatinine0.7 mg/dL
Hepatitis B surface antigen and core antibody; hepatitis C antibodynegative
Hand radiographsperiarticular osteopenia; no erosions
RH-002.lead: In addition to a short course of low-dose prednisone, which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

choices.D: Continue ibuprofen alone and reassess in 6 months

RH-002.explain_html:
Correct answer: C Early rheumatoid arthritis

Symmetric small-joint polyarthritis with prolonged morning stiffness, high-titer RF and anti-CCP and elevated CRP is rheumatoid arthritis with moderate–high disease activity. Anti-CCP is highly specific (~95%) and predicts erosive disease.

The window to prevent joint damage is early. Start a conventional synthetic DMARD now — methotrexate is the anchor drug (start ~15 mg weekly, increase to 20–25 mg weekly, with daily folic acid). Treat to target (remission or low disease activity), reassess every 1–3 months, and add a biologic or targeted synthetic DMARD if the target is not reached in 3–6 months.

Before methotrexate, check CBC, liver tests, creatinine, hepatitis B and C serologies and a chest radiograph; counsel to limit alcohol and use contraception (methotrexate is teratogenic).

Why not the others

  • (A) Adalimumab — TNF inhibitors are added when methotrexate fails to reach target. Monotherapy as the first DMARD is not preferred, and they cost far more.
  • (B) Hydroxychloroquine — Hydroxychloroquine is used for low disease activity or in combination. It is not enough for moderate–high activity RA.
  • (D) Continue ibuprofen alone and reassess in 6 months — NSAIDs relieve symptoms but do not stop erosions. Delaying a DMARD for 6 months risks irreversible damage.
  • (E) Tofacitinib — JAK inhibitors are reserved for inadequate response to methotrexate and carry warnings for VTE, MACE and malignancy (especially age ≥50 with risk factors).
🎓 ABIM pearl

RA spares the DIP joints. DIP involvement points to osteoarthritis (Heberden nodes) or psoriatic arthritis (with nail pitting).

🎯 Educational objective

Start methotrexate (with folic acid) promptly for newly diagnosed moderate–high activity rheumatoid arthritis, using a short glucocorticoid bridge if needed, and escalate by treat-to-target.

RH-003.stem_html:
A 74-year-old woman comes to the office with 3 weeks of a new headache over her right temple. Combing her hair hurts, and her jaw aches after chewing for a minute. She also has aching and stiffness of her shoulders and hips for 1 hour each morning. She has lost 3 kg (6.6 lb) and has had low-grade fevers. Her vision is normal.

Temperature is 37.8 °C (100.0 °F) and blood pressure is 138/80 mm Hg in both arms. The right temporal artery is tender and nodular with a reduced pulse. Visual acuity is 20/25 in both eyes; fundi are normal. Shoulder range of motion is limited by pain; strength is normal.

Erythrocyte sedimentation rate88 mm/h
C-reactive protein6.9 mg/dL
Hemoglobin11.1 g/dL
Platelets468,000/µL
RH-003.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.A: Prednisone 40–60 mg daily now, then temporal artery biopsy or ultrasound
choices.B: Temporal artery biopsy, and start prednisone if the biopsy is positive

RH-003.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Giant cell arteritis

New headache after 50, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, a tender temporal artery, polymyalgia symptoms and very high inflammatory markers = giant cell arteritis (GCA) until proven otherwise.

The feared complication is sudden, permanent vision loss from anterior ischemic optic neuropathy. So: start high-dose glucocorticoids immediately (prednisone 40–60 mg/day; IV methylprednisolone if vision is affected), then confirm with temporal artery biopsy or vascular ultrasound. Biopsy stays diagnostic for at least 1–2 weeks after steroids start.

Add tocilizumab to allow a faster steroid taper (fewer relapses and less steroid toxicity).

Why not the others

  • (B) Temporal artery biopsy, and start prednisone if the biopsy is positive — Waiting for biopsy before treating risks blindness; biopsy findings persist for weeks after steroids start.
  • (C) Aspirin alone — Aspirin is not a substitute for glucocorticoids; its role in preventing ischemic events in GCA is uncertain.
  • (D) Prednisone 15 mg daily — 15 mg is the dose for isolated polymyalgia rheumatica. GCA needs high-dose glucocorticoids.
  • (E) MRI of the brain — Brain MRI does not diagnose GCA and delays treatment. (MRI or CT angiography of the aorta can assess large-vessel GCA later.)
🧠 Mnemonic

GCA red flags — "JAW HuRTS": Jaw claudication, Age >50, Worse vision, Headache (new), Rheumatica (PMR), Tender Scalp.

🎓 ABIM pearl

About half of patients with GCA have PMR, and about 15% of patients with PMR develop GCA. Ask every PMR patient about headache, jaw claudication and vision at every visit.

🎯 Educational objective

When giant cell arteritis is suspected, start high-dose glucocorticoids immediately and confirm the diagnosis with temporal artery biopsy or ultrasound afterward.

RH-004.stem_html:
A 38-year-old man who works in a warehouse comes to the office with 5 days of low back pain that began after lifting a heavy box. The pain is in the lower lumbar area and right buttock and does not travel below the knee. It is worse with bending and better lying still. He has no fever, weight loss, history of cancer, injection drug use, bowel or bladder changes, or numbness in the groin.

Temperature is 36.8 °C (98.2 °F). There is right paraspinal muscle tenderness and limited flexion due to pain. Straight-leg raise is negative bilaterally. Strength, sensation and reflexes in both legs are normal.
RH-004.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.B: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug and advice to stay active

RH-004.explain_html:
Correct answer: B Acute low back pain

This is acute nonspecific (mechanical) low back pain with no red flags and a normal neurologic examination. More than 90% of patients improve within 4–6 weeks regardless of treatment.

Management:

  • No imaging for the first 6 weeks without red flags — imaging finds incidental degenerative changes, does not improve outcomes, and leads to more procedures.
  • Stay active; return to normal activity as tolerated.
  • First-line treatments: superficial heat, massage, acupuncture or spinal manipulation; if medication is needed, an NSAID or a short course of a skeletal muscle relaxant.
Red flags → image early Concern
Cancer history, unexplained weight loss Metastasis
Fever, injection drug use, recent infection, immunosuppression Epidural abscess, osteomyelitis
Saddle anesthesia, urinary retention, bilateral leg weakness Cauda equina syndrome
Progressive or severe neurologic deficit Cord or root compression
Osteoporosis, glucocorticoid use, older age with trauma Compression fracture

Why not the others

  • (A) Lumbar spine radiographs — Radiographs expose the patient to radiation and add nothing without red flags.
  • (C) MRI of the lumbar spine — MRI without red flags does not change management and often shows disk bulges unrelated to symptoms. Reserve it for red flags or persistent radiculopathy in a surgical or injection candidate.
  • (D) Bed rest for 1 week — Bed rest slows recovery compared with staying active.
  • (E) Oxycodone for 2 weeks — Opioids are no better than NSAIDs for acute low back pain and carry risks of dependence and harm.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Sciatica (pain below the knee with a positive straight-leg raise) without deficits is also treated conservatively first; most cases improve within 6 weeks.

🎯 Educational objective

Acute low back pain without red flags needs no imaging; treat with activity, heat and NSAIDs or a short muscle-relaxant course.

RH-005.stem_html:
A 54-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus comes to the office with 4 months of gradually worsening pain and stiffness of her left shoulder. She now cannot reach behind her back to fasten her bra or reach a high shelf. The pain wakes her at night when she rolls onto that side. She recalls no injury.

There is no shoulder swelling or warmth. Active and passive range of motion are both markedly reduced in all planes, most severely in external rotation. Strength is normal within the available range. Shoulder radiographs are normal.
RH-005.lead: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
RH-005.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Adhesive capsulitis

The key finding is loss of both active AND passive motion, worst in external rotation, with normal radiographs. That is adhesive capsulitis ("frozen shoulder") — inflammation and fibrosis of the glenohumeral capsule. It is much more common in diabetes and thyroid disease and after periods of immobility.

It runs in phases — freezing (painful), frozen (stiff), thawing — over 1–3 years. Treatment: physical therapy with stretching, NSAIDs, and an intra-articular glucocorticoid injection for pain in the early phase.

Active ROM Passive ROM Clue
Rotator cuff tendinopathy / impingement Painful arc Normal Pain on 60–120° abduction
Rotator cuff tear Reduced, weak Normal Drop-arm sign
Adhesive capsulitis Reduced Reduced External rotation worst, normal X-ray
Glenohumeral OA Reduced Reduced Joint space loss, osteophytes on X-ray

Why not the others

  • (B) Glenohumeral osteoarthritis — Osteoarthritis also limits both active and passive motion, but radiographs would show joint-space narrowing and osteophytes.
  • (C) Rotator cuff tear — A rotator cuff tear limits active motion and strength, but the examiner can move the arm passively through a normal range.
  • (D) Biceps tendinopathy — Biceps tendinopathy causes anterior shoulder pain with tenderness in the bicipital groove and does not restrict passive motion.
  • (E) Subacromial impingement syndrome — Impingement causes a painful arc with preserved passive motion.
🎓 ABIM pearl

If passive motion is lost after a fall in an older adult, get an axillary view — a posterior shoulder dislocation is easily missed and also blocks external rotation.

🎯 Educational objective

Loss of both active and passive shoulder motion, especially external rotation, with normal radiographs indicates adhesive capsulitis, which is associated with diabetes.
